About
Odero Otieno is the Founder, CEO, and CTO of Dipp AI Technologies based in New York, where he leads the company to close the gap between AI's reasoning capability and enterprises' ability to trust it with real execution at scale.

Odero founded Dipp AI Technologies to answer a critical question he encountered repeatedly across enterprise AI deployments: not whether an organization could adopt AI, but whether it could execute with AI safely, accountably, cost effectively, provably and in control of their own data.

He pioneered Human-in-the-Role and built Orcher, the unified architecture that delivers execution authority alongside disciplined economics, provable data control, and continuous observability as one integrated system rather than four separate initiatives.

Odero’s approach to dynamic model routing addresses a core enterprise risk: binding a platform to one heavy frontier model wastes tokens and leaks proprietary data. Dipp AI’s strategy decouples orchestration from any single provider, matching each task to the cheapest model that can carry it while keeping prompts and data strictly inside the enterprise's own tenant boundary.

Before founding Dipp AI, Odero spent a decade in senior engineering leadership at Fortune 100 scale:

At Humana: Served as Managing Director of Engineering for Cloud, Data, and AI Platforms, architecting infrastructure supporting more than $130 billion in annual revenue and 20 million-plus customers across healthcare, insurance, and finance.

At Microsoft: Served as Principal Director of Software Engineering for Enterprise Platforms, leading platform engineering for the company's top 100 enterprise customers.

At Texas Medical Center: Served as Technical Fellow and Founder in Residence, building economic and data infrastructure for the $25 billion annual revenue medical complex.

At DawaSwift: Co-founded and led the on-demand medicine delivery platform as Chief Executive Officer and Technical Lead.

Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) fails at enterprise scale in frontier AI. In a well documented incident in July, a human reviewer was actively watching and approving every agent action in a live coding session. Roughly forty benign file writes were approved in sequence before the destructive one arrived, and the forty-first - which dropped a production database - received the same review as the first. 

The expert was actively supervising every action an AI coding agent took, in real time, and a production database still got deleted. The failure was not attention. It was architecture. 

Human-in-the-Role (HITR), pionered at Dipp AI Technologies would have checked that command against the reviewer's actual authority to authorize a destructive production change, independent of how many prior approvals had already happened.

We need to have an honest conversation about "Human-in-the-Loop." 

It sounds responsible on a slide deck, but in a live production environment under heavy volume, it completely breaks down. 

When you pipe thousands of automated agent proposals into a review queue, human psychology takes over. Reviewers suffer from automation bias. Under time pressure, they burn out, miss edge cases, and rely on timeout-auto-proceed just to clear their screens. Studies show that when presented with incorrect AI advice, human accuracy drops from 82% to under 46%. 

A 30-second review window is not a security control. It’s a bottleneck that encourages blind rubber-stamping.

Enterprise AI needs structural enforcement, not passive oversight. That means moving to **Human-in-the-Role (HITR)**:
- Directives are issued by a named professional, not an anonymous prompt.
- Authority, scope, and entitlements are cryptographically bound *before* any model executes.
- Halt is the default. If an action falls outside authorized parameters, it cannot run—there is nothing to rubber-stamp.
- Every single cycle hashes directly into a tamper-evident audit ledger that regulators can trust.

Control belongs at execution, not at review. Read our complete analysis in *The Enterprise Superintelligence Report, Vol. I*: https://lnkd.in/dtW89ZVC… more

Yesterday was the deadline for merchants to claim a piece of Discover's $1.225 billion settlement.

The allegation: Discover misclassified consumer cards as commercial cards, silently overcharging merchants on every swipe for 17 years.

When I tell people that most vertical SaaS platforms have no real visibility into their underlying payment fees, I usually get a polite nod and a "yeah, we should probably look into that." This settlement is why I don't find that nod reassuring.

It's not that processors are villains. It's that the fee structure is dense enough, and the reporting opaque enough, that systematic overcharges can run for nearly two decades before a class action forces the issue into daylight.

How confident are you that your current payment reporting would catch something like this?

Stripe announced 288 products at Sessions. I watched most of it.

Genuine reaction: impressive. The agentic commerce direction is ambitious, and the Google partnership is a real market signal. Stripe is clearly building for a world where AI agents transact autonomously and they're moving fast.

The shipped feature that actually caught my attention was network cost passthrough. It's a capability for platforms to pass interchange and scheme fees to their merchants instead of charging a blended rate.

It's a good thing. But it only passes on the same black box of fees to merchants that prefer predictability, and are poorly equipped to decipher payment economics.

That's the gap worth talking about. As payments become more programmable and AI-native, transparency can’t be optional. Passing through network costs is a step forward but merchants still need clarity on why fees change, what’s negotiable, and what influences downgrades and penalties from the card networks. That’s top of mind for us at Fluxmap.

Stop downloading LLMs your machine was never going to run.

llmfit scans your hardware and tells you exactly which models will run. 

It scans your RAM, CPU, GPU, and VRAM first.

1. Quality, based on parameter count and quantization
2. Speed, estimating tokens per second for your exact backend
3. Fit, matching memory use to your hardware
4. Context window support for your use case 

Each model gets a label: Perfect, Good, Marginal, or Too Tight. 

It picks the best quantization automatically, stepping down until something fits.

🔹 Job postings demand production streaming experience.
🔹 But you need a job to access production streaming systems.
🔹 And you can't practice with real user data due to privacy regulations (GDPR, etc.).

I couldn't find a good way to get hands-on experience, so I built my own end-to-end streaming system with synthetic data.

🔧 Key features of the project:
• Real-time data generation (70-column validated user records) via Server-Sent Events (SSE).
• Automated API key management with tiered access and expiration.
• A live, real-time fraud detection dashboard (Random Forest) that classifies incoming data instantly.
• A resilient local fallback generator to guarantee 100% uptime, even if external LLM APIs are rate-limited.

The goal was twofold: create a realistic practice environment for devs in similar situations, and provide a lightweight tool for teams to stress-test ML ingestion pipelines.

A personalized mRNA vaccine for pancreatic cancer has shown remarkable potential in clinical trials.

It triggered long-lasting immune responses that could prevent the disease from ever returning.

For decades, pancreatic cancer has been one of the most lethal and difficult-to-treat malignancies, notorious for its high recurrence rate even after successful surgical removal.

However, a groundbreaking Phase 1 clinical trial of a personalized mRNA vaccine, known as autogene cevumeran, offers a beacon of hope.

Led by researchers at the Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, the trial evaluated the vaccine’s ability to train patients' immune systems to recognize and destroy microscopic, post-surgery cancer cells. The vaccine works by analyzing each patient’s tumor to identify specific mutations, creating a custom mRNA blueprint that prompts the body to produce cancer-fighting T cells.

The results have been remarkably encouraging: the vaccine successfully triggered a robust, long-lasting immune response in half of the study participants.

Follow-up data presented in 2026 revealed that those patients who mounted an immune response experienced a significantly lower risk of cancer recurrence, with nearly 90% of these 'responders' still alive up to six years post-treatment.

This milestone marks a critical shift toward proactive, highly targeted cancer interception and paves the way for larger clinical trials aimed at transforming the prognosis for pancreatic cancer patients worldwide.

Great conversation between Lenny Rachitsky and Adam Ward (Head of Talent Cursor) on what Adam calls the hiring “funnel of doom”.
 
Simply, the traditional hiring funnel is optimized for volume rather than precision.

Volume is easy to measure, i.e. applications received / invites / interviews / offers, but it results in a “remainder-based” hiring framework where you’re choosing from whoever survives the funnel, not necessarily maximizing your odds of finding the best candidates. 

There are layers to the doom:
👉 𝗝𝗼𝗯 𝗯𝗼𝗮𝗿𝗱𝘀 𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗺𝗼𝘀𝘁 𝗲𝘅𝗽𝗼𝘀𝗲𝗱. There’s almost no targeting at the top of the funnel. Anyone can apply, and AI has made that worse through auto-appliers and fake applications.
👉 𝗢𝘂𝘁𝗯𝗼𝘂𝗻𝗱 𝗰𝗮𝗻 𝗳𝗮𝗹𝗹 𝗶𝗻𝘁𝗼 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝘀𝗮𝗺𝗲 𝘁𝗿𝗮𝗽 if the strategy is simply “message 1,000 people and work with whoever replies.” You’re not necessarily finding the best talent…
👉 𝗥𝗲𝗳𝗲𝗿𝗿𝗮𝗹𝘀 𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝗵𝗶𝗴𝗵𝗲𝗿 𝘀𝗶𝗴𝗻𝗮𝗹, especially when employees are given a clear picture of what great looks like. But those networks can get exhausted quickly, and most companies still need to hire on a timeline.

Cursor seems to have done particularly well by turning employee networks into a powerful sourcing channel. Internal talent teams would work with employees to identify people in their network who fit the profile, then build relationships over time and eventually pull them in. That can work extremely well when you already have a dense network of top talent. 

The best recruiters can extend that same model beyond a single company because they already have their own networks, CRM history, and market knowledge to know where the strongest candidates are likely to come from.

An AI talent system can amplify that advantage:
✅ 𝗦𝘂𝗿𝗳𝗮𝗰𝗲 𝗰𝗮𝗻𝗱𝗶𝗱𝗮𝘁𝗲𝘀 based on deeper skills, traits, and career patterns
✅ 𝗥𝗲𝗮𝗰𝘁𝗶𝘃𝗮𝘁𝗲 𝗿𝗲𝗹𝗲𝘃𝗮𝗻𝘁 𝗽𝗲𝗼𝗽𝗹𝗲 from past convos
✅ 𝗟𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗻 𝗮 𝗿𝗲𝗰𝗿𝘂𝗶𝘁𝗲𝗿’𝘀 𝗻𝗶𝗰𝗵𝗲, preferences, and “secret sauce”… then apply it to future searches
✅ 𝗖𝗼𝗼𝗿𝗱𝗶𝗻𝗮𝘁𝗲 𝗳𝗼𝗹𝗹𝗼𝘄-𝘂𝗽𝘀, interview context, and personalized touchpoints across the team
✅ 𝗦𝘂𝗿𝗳𝗮𝗰𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗿𝗶𝗴𝗵𝘁 𝗺𝗼𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁𝘀 𝘁𝗼 𝗿𝗲-𝗲𝗻𝗴𝗮𝗴𝗲 based on job changes, company moves, or new opportunities

As modern solutions bring better memory, timing, context, and targeting, the “funnel of doom” should give way to identifying the right people earlier, engaging them more intentionally, and building stronger relationships over time.… more

This dynamic puts more pressure on HR and recruiting teams to present clearer, more structured information that actually supports decision-making. No more hunches.

This is giving them a clear edge, both in how they present candidates and in the credibility of their process. It also equips them with tangible data points, allowing them to quickly recalibrate and target new candidate profiles when needed.

Point blank... the market now demands a higher level of precision and intelligence across both client and talent acquisition.

The bar has moved.

My biggest takeaways from expert comp negotiator Jacob Warwick:

1. A very soft pushback can materially change your offer. Jacob’s simplest line is “What’s the chance there’s a little more here?” He says he often sees roughly 20% movement from that alone, across everything from earlier-stage roles to seven-figure roles. 

2. Jacob typically looks for around 40% movement when a negotiation is run well. Most candidates are negotiating far too narrowly because they’re reacting to the first number, the first band, or the first title they hear instead of building leverage throughout the process.

3. Product leaders, engineers, and designers often negotiate worse than louder functions. Jacob’s observation is that thoughtful, introverted, highly competent people tend to over-index on being reasonable and under-index on testing the ceiling. Meanwhile, more extroverted functions are often more comfortable treating negotiation as part of the job.

4. Great negotiation is collaborative, not adversarial. This came up repeatedly, and it is probably the biggest misconception the episode corrects. Jacob is not teaching people to beat companies. He is teaching them to better understand the value at stake and structure a deal that reflects it, sometimes through salary, sometimes through equity, and sometimes through more creative mechanisms like milestone-based compensation.

5. Your first comp number often becomes your ceiling. This may have been the most useful tactical point in the whole conversation. The danger of naming your number too early is that you are anchoring before you understand the actual scope of the job. By the time you’ve gone through the interview loop, you may realize the company is really hiring for a much bigger role than the original job description suggested. But if you already gave a number, that old number can get used against you.

6. Information + timing create power. This is the backbone of his whole system. Slow the process down. Ask better questions. Create more surface area for understanding what the company needs, who the internal champions are, and where the actual constraints sit. The more rushed you feel, the weaker your position usually is.

We have posted previously on various surveillance related subjects. Physical surveillance is the ‘direct observation of people, vehicles, or activity taking place at some given location for the purpose of obtaining information’. When surveillance operators conduct tasks an import basic skill is to be able to accurately describe the appearance of a person, a skill most surveillance operators are highly proficient at. Yes, surveillance operators, the police, military and other organisations are trained in this skill, but It’s also a skill we can all benefit from and may need – you may witness an incident (criminal or something else) and be questioned by the police in regard to the people you saw taking part in the incident. Information you witness and subsequently describe may prove vital to the police enabling them to apprehend criminal suspects or piece together an event. 

As with most dynamic situations it’s easy to miss key information, get caught up in watching an incident without actually taking anything in. In most situations (if safe to do so) the main thing to do is focus on the people involved and what they are doing. Key physical features of a human are - height, weight, size, shape or other bodily characteristic. These also include facial features - hair, scarring and birthmarks. Physical features may also include piercings, tattoos or body modifications. Clearly mobile phone cameras are a tool that you can/could use when witnessing an incident, but it may not always be possible or appropriate leaving you to rely on the naked eye.

🧐 Technical interview tip #2: be interested.

Have you ever gotten to the part of an interview where you are supposed to ask questions, and you either don't know what to say, or fall back on a generic "what's the day of a developer like there?" This tip's for you.

When you've been looking long enough, it's easy to internalize an attitude something like "I'll take anything." All applications and interviewers start to blur together; pass a test => get a job. But this (very common) early-career failure mode will make it far tougher to sustain yourself through the process long enough, or with enough energy, to get any job. If you do get one, you might quickly find yourself bored, dreading work, and searching again rather quickly. But now with a short stint and notable lack of achievements to explain.

Instead, seemingly against the odds, start with your interests. Set aside desperation, and peel back any layers of preemptive self-defense against failure or cynical coping strategies. Recall why you got into tech in the first place, and what kinds problems you find inherently fascinating. What did you actually want to be when you grew up? What are the qualities of people that you most want to work with? For real. Type this up in detail.

Now search for companies that actually work on the problems you care about. Yes, feel free to use an LLM too, but use it to broaden out from your deep interests with something like this prompt:

"Here are the problems I care about, the things I like to work on, and qualities of collaborators I seek. I am searching for work as a developer at a company where these will be in great alignment. In case I can't find work that's an exact fit, what are some fields and specific companies that might be a creative close fit; that is companies where my interests and predilections will generalize nicely:

```
{your actual career interests, hopes, needs, and dreams}
```
"

(Yes, the specific language matters here. You are prompting both yourself and the LLM for optimism, creativity, and precision.)

Start with the resulting list of companies in your search. Write down the questions you have about each of them, before you even apply. You should find yourself in a very different mindset: curious and excited to learn how they do it, and where they need help to scale their impact.

Remember that any interviewer and future team worth your time is looking for three things: 1) evidence you can do the job, 2) evidence they want to spend a lot of time with you, 3) and evidence you are aligned with and interested enough in what specifically has to be done in THIS role at THIS company to solve problems with infectious energy and increasing independence.

1) is why you went to school/bootcamp but 2) and 3) are so much easier when you start with what you inherently care about. Be interested to be interesting.

↩️ Coding interview tip #1: always follow up.

Sometimes interviews go OK, sometimes not 🤢. But either way, maximize learning and improve your chances by following up. That doesn't just mean an email, though. Try these steps:

1. Reserve an hour the same day of the interview to capture the problem verbatim and solve it again. Resist the temptation to run away and forget about a suboptimal interview. Definitely also avoid the cheap victory of a googled/AI-generated solution! You'll almost always see something you didn't in the heat of the interview when you review again: keep notes and write a better solution. Over time, build a library of these problems for your own practice. Questions you've been exposed to under real interview stress hit different, and help you learn faster.

2. Now follow up with your interviewer. Sometimes you'll hear back, sometimes not, but that's not your goal: any interviewer I've ever asked appreciates a simple (short) note of thanks. Something like "Hey Jeff Dean, thanks for your time today. I enjoyed the conversation and working on FizzBuzz together. While I got it done, I played around with the problem afterwards, and realized a for loop and a few modulo checks might have been more elegant than a thousand if/elses.  Thanks again! -Patrick." Remember this is not a test at school: you're a future colleague, expressing gratitude for someone else's time and attention, and demonstrating that you learn from experience.

3. Do the problem again from scratch the next day to reinforce what you've learned and internalize the feeling of successful problem solving.

🙅Things to avoid: don't assume you did poorly and argue with your own impression of the interviewer's judgment for a better outcome. Those are not fun follow-up emails to read. Don't publish the interview question (it's pretty easy to tell sometimes which particular candidate does this, and it's a good way to annoy your potential team). Above all, don't spiral: solving technical questions is a very learnable skill with practice. The main obstacles are negative self-labeling ("I'm not good at coding interviews") and other kinds of discouraging inner monologue.

That's it! It's an achievement worth celebrating to even get a coding interview, and these steps will help you learn more from the experience, gain or reestablish momentum, and create a habit of diligence and gratitude (which is a lot more important than the ability to one-shot algorithm/data structure problems in software jobs, anyways).

---

There are many varieties of this kind of learning; you can use a familiar interview problem to start learning a new programming language, fill in gaps in your education, test AI models and agents' relative performance, learn about testing methodologies...

2,18 € de Doliprane. 12 000 € de dégâts. Un couteau. Et un procès dans plus de 7 mois.

Un homme s’est présenté dans notre pharmacie pour demander un Doliprane.

Il avait son attestation de carte Vitale, mais pas d’ordonnance. Mon pharmacien lui explique simplement que sans ordonnance, le médicament n’est pas remboursé et qu’il faut donc payer 2,18 €.

Il a préféré fracasser notre vitrine.

Mais le plus grave est ailleurs : il voulait en découdre avec mon pharmacien.

Des passants ont eu le courage de s’interposer. Je veux les remercier publiquement : ils ont probablement évité un drame et ont eux-mêmes pris un risque considérable puisque l’individu a sorti un couteau.

La police l’a interpellé et je remercie les agents pour leur intervention.

Il a ensuite été placé en centre de rétention administrative.

Son jugement ?

Le 30 mars 2027.

Soit plus de 7 mois après les faits.

Et c’est là que je m’interroge.

Pourquoi attendre aussi longtemps pour juger quelqu’un interpellé après des faits aussi graves ?

D’ici mars, sera-t-il encore en France ? Libre ? Et surtout : se présentera-t-il réellement devant le tribunal ?

Je ne peux pas affirmer qu’il ne viendra pas.

Mais une chose est certaine : moi, victime, je serai là.

Avec les photos. Avec les factures.
Avec environ 12 000 € de réparations.

Et cette histoire me rappelle malheureusement 2022.

Un individu avait déjà cassé notre vitrine après le refus d’une Ventoline sans ordonnance.

Plus de 10 000 € de dégâts.

Sauf qu’à la suite d’une erreur de procédure, c’est moi qui ai été désigné comme le prévenu.

Résultat : condamné à 170 € d’amende (si peu ?) pour avoir soi-disant cassé la vitrine de ma propre pharmacie.

J’ai signalé l’erreur. On m’a assuré qu’elle serait corrigée.

Quatre ans plus tard, l’amende était passée à 201 € et, le 10 avril 2026, l’État a prélevé directement ces 201 € sur mon compte par saisie administrative.

J’étais la victime et j’ai fini par payer l’amende.

À ce jour, je n’ai toujours pas été remboursé.

Je ne critique pas les policiers : ils interviennent, interpellent et font leur travail.

Ma question est ailleurs :

Que fait-on réellement pour les victimes après ?

Combien d’années de procédures ?
Combien d’argent avancé ?
Et pourquoi attendre des mois pour juger des faits impliquant une arme ?

Aujourd’hui, qui paiera les 12 000 € si l’auteur est insolvable ?

Et surtout, faudra-t-il attendre qu’un pharmacien, un salarié ou un passant soit poignardé pour considérer le problème comme suffisamment grave ?

En 2022 : une vitrine cassée, plus de 10 000 € de dégâts et 201 € prélevés sur le compte de la victime.

En 2026 : 2,18 € de Doliprane refusé, environ 12 000 € de dégâts et un couteau sorti.

Jusqu’à quand ?

(Je publierai dans un second post les vidéos de l’agression, LinkedIn ne permettant pas de les intégrer ici)

Personne n'en parle, et pourtant cet outil vient de diviser mes temps de build par deux.

Il s'appelle RNRepo, et il règle un truc absurde que tu fais sans le savoir.

À chaque build, tu recompiles Reanimated, Skia, gesture-handler...
Du code que tu n'as jamais écrit ni touché.

Et tu n'es pas seul.

Partout dans le monde, des machines recompilent en boucle EXACTEMENT les mêmes fichiers.
Pour produire des binaires strictement identiques.

Des millions de fois par jour. Pour rien.

Et ce problème est DÉJÀ résolu ailleurs.

En Android natif, tu télécharges tes libs pré-compilées via Maven.
Côté JS, pareil avec npm.
Tu ne recompiles pas, tu télécharges le binaire.

Alors pourquoi pas en React Native ?

C'est la question que pose RNRepo, de Software Mansion.

L'idée : un dépôt de binaires natifs pré-compilés pour l'écosystème RN.
Au lieu de recompiler Reanimated à chaque build, tu télécharges la version déjà compilée et signée.

Résultat : des builds jusqu'à 2x plus rapides.

Mais pourquoi personne ne l'avait fait avant ?

Parce qu'il y a une vraie subtilité.

Beaucoup de libs embarquent du C++ et se lient à une version SPÉCIFIQUE de React Native.
Donc un binaire pré-compilé ne marche que pour cette version exacte de RN.

Le publier à la main voudrait dire recompiler pour chaque version de RN, à chaque sortie.
Ingérable.

La solution de RNRepo est maligne.

Un cron surveille les nouvelles versions de libs ET de React Native.
Il compile automatiquement toute la matrice (lib × version de RN) dans des workflows isolés.

Le mainteneur de la lib n'a RIEN à faire.
C'est 100% transparent pour lui.

Et comme on télécharge des binaires, chaque artefact est signé GPG et traçable jusqu'à son commit.
La vitesse, pas au prix de la confiance.

Petite nuance pour rester honnête.

Le "2x" est un plafond, pas une garantie.
Et si une lib n'est pas pré-compilable, ça retombe simplement sur la compilation classique.
Tes builds ne cassent jamais, ils sont juste plus lents pour ces libs-là.

Le plus intéressant, c'est le mouvement de fond.

Le core RN bascule DÉJÀ vers le pré-compilé (0.80, 0.81, jusqu'à 10x plus rapide sur iOS).
On arrête de compiler depuis les sources.

Le core l'a fait pour lui-même.
RNRepo le fait pour tout le reste de l'écosystème.… more

Most ML serving infrastructure is designed for interactive inference: a request comes in, and the system is expected to return an answer almost immediately.

But much of our ML workload looks different. Our enrichment inference is driven primarily by data pipelines, and the results are consumed downstream rather than in an interactive request-response loop. That means many workloads can tolerate minutes of latency rather than milliseconds.

Once we designed around that actual latency budget, we were able to simplify the system substantially.

The result is Millrace: durable, batched inference that scales against queued work, moves workloads to CPU where it makes sense, and is substantially simpler to operate and deploy.

Along the way, we also learned that parts of our original Ray-based architecture were more sophisticated than the workload actually required.

Jeffrey Kiske and Nicholas Renninger walk through the evolution from Ray Serve to Millrace, what we over-engineered along the way, and why sometimes the right infrastructure move is to delete capabilities you no longer need.

Last week, I locked myself in a room with a small group from our team to review the Karias product roadmap. I walked away with one overwhelming thought... This is wild.

Somewhere along the way Karias evolved from healthcare services company into an end-to-end technology-enabled platform tackling some of the biggest problems in healthcare.

Sometimes I laugh and say, "I have no idea how we got here..." 

Although, if I'm honest, I know exactly how we got here. Just look up.

I don't laugh because I doubt the vision. Quite the opposite. I feel called to steward it. It's a conviction that lives in my heart and can only come from something far bigger than myself.

What makes me laugh is that I don't think in wireframes, engineering sprints, or product architecture. I probably drive our product team crazy with all the questions they ask to pull the vision out of my head because I don't think about software. I think about people.

I think about the overwhelmed mom trying to figure out where to take her child for an MRI. 
The employee staring at a medical bill they don't understand. 
The family trying to make one of the biggest financial decisions of their lives with almost no information.

For years, my brain has been a constant stream of ideas about how those moments should feel different. They rarely come out in neat, logical order. 

They're voice memos recorded while driving. Scribbles in GoodNotes. Whiteboard sketches. Random messages. Half-finished thoughts that suddenly connect to another problem because healthcare is one giant interconnected experience. My team has learned to interrupt me and say, "Let me record this."

Last week, they did something incredible. They took months of conversations, voice notes, whiteboard sessions, and my jumbled train of thought and transformed them into a product roadmap that was elegant, intentional, and connected.

Every capability leads naturally to the next.
Every feature solves another point of friction.
Every interaction gives people something they've never had in healthcare: understanding, confidence, and agency.

There was a moment where I sat back and thought: "Is this really happening?"

It's such a privilege to work alongside a team that can take a founder's messy vision and translate it into something tangible, something that has the potential to change how millions of people experience healthcare.

That's the beauty of building.

The founder doesn't have to know how to write every line of code. The founder has to relentlessly understand the problems worth solving and never lose sight of the people on the other side of the screen.

I'm incredibly grateful for our product and engineering teams, whose talent continues to amaze me every day. They take ideas that begin as passion and purpose and turn them into reality.

We're building something special. Something bigger than we ever imagined when we started. And for the opportunity to steward it... I'll never stop being grateful.… more

Digitization or Digitalization??? (Is that even a word?)

So I learnt two pretty cool things this year that could possibly benefit a couple of people and organizations. (actually 3 things come to think of it)

1) The difference between digitization and digitalization (I always thought digitalization was just bad English haha 🥹 #RIPtoMe).
2) The benefit of digitizing and then digitalizing on a per mining crew basis.
3) The fact that you can publish your cool PowerBI dashboard / report, that no one cares about, to the web for people to view and interact with (digitalization at its best).

So this is what I have learnt and perhaps it can help you.

1) Digitization vs Digitalization ???

Digitization is the act of installing instrumentation which enables you to gather data and information about your operation.

Digitalization is the act of taking that information out of the historian / database / archives and turning it into a useful report or dashboard from which decisions can be made.

2) Digitizing and then Digitalizing on a per mining crew basis

First we measured - with our compressed air flow meters, water meters and power meters. One data point every second for a whole month.

Then we processed - Data to PC, PC to SQL Server, Server to PowerBI. (this was quite literally too much data to even be opened in excel).

Then we discussed - What does this cool data on this cool dashboard tell us?

To name a few things:

1 - Total Utility Consumption - which leads to a cost per crew $$$ (show me the money). This leads to accountability. When we are wasting, why are we wasting?

2 - Quality of Utility supply to end user - which leads to productivity of the crew. Do they have sufficient CA pressure, yes or no? Do they have sufficient water supply, yes or no? Are the environmental conditions good, yes or no? Is the power supplied to this area of a high quality, yes or no? If one of these is an issue, what can we do to fix it?

3 - Efficiency and effectiveness of the crew - What time do they start? What time do they stop? How many holes did they drill? Are they flushing the raise lines with water causing a mudrush? Should they really be booking a blast today? If any of these are any issue, why is it an issue and what can we do to address it?

4 - Can we Forecast Production? Yes! Are we on track for this months call? Probably not haha, why not? Roof bolting is too slow...

These are just some examples of where this data led us.

Most mining “digital twins” fail and this isn’t because the tech sucks—it’s because too few people see them as living systems.

I got asked recently:
“What is a digital twin in the mining context?”

and it compelled me to think: the problem isn’t the concept—it’s the execution and maintenance.

In mining, a digital twin is (or at least should be) a real-time, dynamic replica of your compressed air, service water, ventilation network (or other simulatable processes) — from surface all the way to where it matters most, the reef horizon. 

It is supposed to enable us to run as many "what if" scenarios about your infrastructure as you want, without spending a cent on CAPex (this doesn't include the cost of the consultant who builds the simulation of course ;) ) 

Want to change your compressed air pipes in the haulage from an 8" to a 10"?

Got it, that will increase your reef horizon pressures at peak drilling shift by 1.5 bar and should lead to a 50% reduction in lost blasts. 

Did you need to deploy any capital to figure that out? 

No... 

But here’s where most trip up: They build the twin and walk away. 

No updates and no live sensors which tie into the digital twin to keep it up to date... 

Underground changes happen—valves shift, new pipes get added—but nobody tells the model.

The twin quickly becomes a snapshot of a past reality. A mine that once was...

Not actionable. Not reliable. Just digital dust.

A real digital twin lives off live data. It stays accurate, useful—and gives you answers without sending countless engineering consultants underground to audit for months on end or burning CapEx.

The life of a true digital twin starts with digitization... and ends with informed decisions. 

are you running a living twin, or just something gathering digital dust?

Our mission is to make medical travel transparent, trustworthy, and accessible by giving every patient the information and confidence they need to make informed healthcare decisions.
As an Estonia-based early-stage HealthTech startup, we are committed to building long-term partnerships with verified clinics while creating a trusted digital ecosystem for international patients.

💁‍♀️ The Ukrainian digital envoys of the e-Governance Academy (eGA) had a friendly meeting with US Ambassador to Estonia, George P. Kent.

💻 In addition to facilitating the use of everyday Estonian and Ukrainian e-services, the digital envoys from Ukraine also played a crucial role in familiarizing local Ukrainians with digital tools and solutions.

📍 Tartu Help Bot: A Telegram bot providing essential information to Ukrainian refugees regarding refugee status and integration resources.
📍 Scam Map: A visual guide highlighting common fraud schemes and preventive measures to safeguard the Ukrainian community in Estonia from financial and psychological harm.
📍 Professional Development Workshop: Workshops aimed at equipping Ukrainians with essential digital skills for success in the Estonian job market.
📍 Easy Stuudium: A project facilitating the use of essential educational programs for Ukrainian children and their parents in Estonia.

"For eGA, which primarily operates outside Estonia, this is our unique opportunity to collaborate within Estonia for the benefit of the Ukrainian people," said Kristina Mänd, lead of the project.

💡 In the first cohort, eGA engaged 31 talented young Ukrainians living in Estonia, training them as digital envoys, who have since reached over 10,000 Ukrainians, educating and empowering over 400 digitally vulnerable community members.

The project DEUCE, or “Digital Empowerment of the Ukrainian Community in Estonia”, is slated to continue until September 2025 and is being implemented by eGA with support from the United States Department of State, totaling $236,000.

These past two days, stellar // welcomed David Patiashvili, part of the Tiple network, to work with two STEER®'s engineers on integrating AI concretely into their practices.

Goal: better practices, improved workflows, automation, and integration with a local AI model to reduce token consumption on tasks like code review and testing activities.
 
One concrete example of what came out of it: an automated review flow used for a huge merge request (99 files, 200k+ diff). Claude Code triggers the automation in n8n (the workflow itself built with Claude), which relies on a local Qwen 3.6 model. Ten minutes later, the result lands back in our Gitlab. The engineer still owns the final call, but knows exactly where to focus. Direct gain: probably nearly a half day of boring work avoided, with only real software engineering remaining.
 
More flows like this one are already in the works.
 
Teams that learn to make the most of these tools, without losing their engineering standards, will have a very concrete edge in the years ahead.

Documentation is messy, but we have made it effortless!
 
This Wednesday Elliot Gestrin, Henrik Ahlinder, Josef Olsson, Gaspar Grikainis, Douglas Wiberg and I participated as team Eagles in the Nordic Software Hackathon 2025 as a part of the Monterro Nordic Software Summit at Stockholm Waterfront Congress Centre, powered by Cillers. The past two months we literally hovered like eagles to dive like falcons - resulting in winning the hackathon in front of 1 200 executives!
 
Growing up and living in Linköping, it feels natural with security. I still remembered an AI hackathon ceremony I watched, where someone recorded all the demos and recreated them all in one hour afterwards – imagine that happening for security critical companies like Saab. We therefor pivoted towards a secure, user-controlled recording device and a target-specific AI.
 
On stage I was asked about our winning recipe and the answer is iteration. After weeks of work we pitched at Google Cloud, realizing our chosen pivot was an offline equivalent to Google’s Agentspace. I speak on behalf of the team and from my heart that our awakening came from our meeting with Peter Molander from Google Cloud. With a questioning attitude and great carrying, Peter spent 4 hours with us after work pushing our pivot to the absolute. We realized that the market for our offline solution was fairly small for the audience at Monterro. We left the meeting devastated over our idea, yet infinitely thankful for shaping our mindset – it is the persistence that matters.
 
Two burgers later, around 11 pm, we pivoted from our solution to Docmatic - turning messy documentation into living, AI-powered microlearning. Docmatic is built for adaptation, adoption, and integration - seamlessly transformable to your existing infrastructure! Meaning we superposition the symbiosis in your current infrastructure, supporting both humans and AI agents, while sustaining and improving your current preferences.
 
A big thanks for the teams' presentations! An incredibly big thanks to Per Lange, Peder Linder, Mårten Blixt and Ellinor Nilsson at Cillers along with Monterro and volunteers for creating this world class event! It was a true pleasure pitching for you Katarina Noén from Ericsson, Patrik Hedljung from Scania Group, Ebba Heselius from AI Sweden, Henrik Jarleskog from Sodexo, Frida Monsén from Vattenfall, Johanna Bolin Tingvall from Spotify, Henrik Atteryd from Tele2, Danny Larsson from Google and Amir Elion from Think Big Leaders!
 
To the Jury and the 210+ executives voting for us or anyone else interested – let us book a meeting via our website:

Government is the wildcard the AI conversation treats as background scenery. That treatment is the diligence error of the cycle. The largest single variable affecting which AI profit pools survive and which compress is policy — export controls, compliance regimes, antitrust enforcement, M&A scrutiny, sovereign-AI procurement, the wildcards that follow an administration change or a national-security incident. Nothing in the technology layer rivals it for magnitude.

The largest US AI vendors are spending real capital trying to influence the wildcard. Anthropic disclosed four million nine hundred and forty thousand dollars in cumulative lobbying spend since 2023 with one million ten thousand dollars in Q3 2025 alone, across roughly thirty-six filings. The Frontier Model Forum ran a coordinated policy push in April 2026. Anthropic's "2028: Two Scenarios" paper landed May 14 reading as policy laundering wrapped in research framing. These are the largest US AI vendors trying to lock in current frontier-vendor advantage via export controls, compliance moats, and third-party testing requirements that favor well-capitalized incumbents.

The historical precedent on lobby-versus-reality is unkind to the lobby. When an industry spends to lock in a position, government tends to act in ways the lobby did not predict. How a Chief Design Officer (yours truly) uses AI to design like an IC. This demo is for any designers that haven't yet embraced AI in their workflow.

I’m one of two designers working on this plugin. I manage an organization of about 40 designers of various flavors, but I still keep myself in the trenches whenever possible. Lynt is one of these efforts.

The examples I share are intentionally very simple to demonstrate how any designer at any level can leverage artificial intelligence to amplify and accelerate their human intelligence.

AI is revolutionizing how we work as designers, yet I think of it more like a renaissance; a return to designing in consideration of the medium in which our designs are rendered, much like we did years ago when I first started.

Arbitrarily, something like 80% of what we do as designers (in the act of designing) is exploration and iteration. For the past decade or more so much of that has happened in Figma and previously Sketch. These are great tools. 

But as a result of designing exclusively in a static environment, many have lost the ability to connect ideation with execution. Handholding your work from start to finish eventually gave way to handing off your work, and we never looked back. 

Artificial intelligence flips all of this on its head, positioning you (the designer) to be the one who first turns your design into code, iterate and iterate again, and experience using your work as users will, literally from day one of your design process. 

All the while freeing our engineering colleagues to focus on the work that only they can do, while designing alongside them.

Senior: "The payment module fails when currency = null because exchangeRate returns undefined. Refactor the validation layer to enforce non-null currency before calculation and add a fallback for legacy records."

Same final output quality.
Massively different efficiency.

Compounding frameworks reduce quality variance.
Judgment still determines efficiency.

In an AI-native world, code is abundant. Tokens cost money. Precision becomes capital efficiency.

Our Leap Wasn’t One AI Coding Agent. It Was Building a Swarm.
I want to share where we are with coding agents and the evolution from single agent → AI compounding framework → swarm.

1️⃣ We started like most teams: Cursor + copilot-style usage.
One engineer → one agent → one output.

Productivity improved at the individual level, but the system didn’t change: reviews stayed heavy, architecture still depended on senior judgment, and edge cases were discovered late.

2️⃣ Then we built an AI Compounding Engineering Framework, a way of working that makes AI outputs compound. Clear PRDs + reusable artifacts, a shared memory layer, and reinforcement loops via review checklists and lessons learned.

3️⃣ A couple of months ago, we made a bigger move. We migrated to Claude and stopped treating AI like a helper.  We started building what we actually needed: a role-based swarm.

Swarm structure that’s working for us:
	•	Planner/Architect → PRD → plan + risks
	•	Implementers (2–3) → competing approaches in parallel
	•	QA/Breaker → edge cases + tests
	•	Reviewer/Gatekeeper → score outputs + enforce merge checklist
The engineer stopped prompting. The engineer started orchestrating.

 ✅ What’s working (so far):
	1.	Output quality got consistent: cleaner diffs, better tests, fewer regressions.
	2.	Speed improved where it counts (merge → deploy): drafts aren’t always faster, but rework and review loops dropped.
	3.	Tokens went up, total cost went down: more compute up front, less senior time debugging and rewriting.

❌ What’s challenging: 
We tested going swarm without the compounding framework, and it gets chaotic fast, assumptions drift, architectures diverge, QA feedback doesn’t propagate cleanly, and orchestration overhead eats the gains. Culturally, juniors/mids adapt faster; some seniors need a couple of weeks because the job shifts from writing the code to designing the system and selecting winners.

⭐Summary:
We’re still refining the playbook. But this is the first change that feels structural: AI as a workforce, not an assistant. The unit of labor isn’t the agent. It’s the swarm.

- Don’t try to go swarm-first without a compounding framework. Without shared artifacts + memory, swarms get chaotic fast. 

- Also expect cultural resistance; the job shifts from writing code to designing the system, which can take some teams a couple of weeks to adapt.

💡 What makes this elegant from an architectural standpoint is the directionality of learning. The AI's confusion is not a failure to suppress, but a 𝐝𝐢𝐬𝐜𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐲 𝐦𝐞𝐜𝐡𝐚𝐧𝐢𝐬𝐦. 

It tells you exactly which concepts lack sufficient formal definition in your organisation: something data governance teams have been trying to surface for years through workshops and surveys, with limited success.

Instead of "how mature is our data catalog?", ask "how tight is our feedback loop between agent behaviour and semantic layer evolution?"

A static ontology, however comprehensive, cannot converge. Only a system with a dynamic loop will. That's a solvable engineering problem, and it's the right one to be working on.

Ontologies can save you tokens (the small chunks of text AI models process) and therefore save you money in the age of AI.
 
I have been blowing through token limits building multi-agent systems. It has given me another reason to care about ontologies.
 
Agents spend tokens working out what things mean, finding the right information, and explaining it to one another. A shared ontology can reduce how much of that work they repeat.
 
There are two parts to this.
 
🔵 Be Precise About What You Mean
 
Consider a question: “Which customers have contracts expiring next month?”
 
Does “customer” mean a legal entity, a billing account or a parent company? Does “expiry” mean the end of the contract term or the deadline for giving notice?
 
Without shared definitions, agents have to resolve those ambiguities from whatever context they can find. Two agents can reach different interpretations, then spend more tokens trying to reconcile them.
 
An ontology makes those distinctions explicit. Give agents access to the same definitions and identifiers, and they have less to reconstruct and explain each time.
 
You still need to supply the relevant definitions. The saving comes from reusing precise meaning across tasks, rather than asking the model to infer it afresh.
 
🔵 Build the Roads
 
An organisation is a vast search space. The answer to that contract question might span a CRM, a contract repository and a billing system.
 
A knowledge graph provides a road network between them.
 
Customer → contracting entity → contract → expiry date → source record.
 
The ontology defines what those relationships mean. The graph connects the actual entities and points to the records where the detail lives.
 
The documents and tables can stay in their source systems. An authorised agent follows the relevant connections instead of opening every document that happens to mention the customer.
 
That can mean fewer retrieval calls, less irrelevant context and fewer attempts to get the answer right.
 
There is a cost to building and maintaining this structure. It has to earn its keep. I would judge it on cost per correct answer across repeated tasks, including that maintenance.
 
I want my agents spending their tokens on the question I asked, rather than rediscovering how my organisation works from scratch every time.

One important caveat: NOOA can execute LLM-generated Python, so NVIDIA explicitly recommends OS-level sandboxing rather than relying on its in-process checks.

I thought I understood GPU utilization until I started working on this handbook.

I kept collapsing three different things into one mental picture => the work a kernel launches, the work that is actually resident on the GPU, and the work that is ready to issue right now. They are not the same thing.

Take a kernel with 240 blocks and 256 threads per block. That is 61,440 logical threads, or 1,920 NVIDIA warps. But those warps are not all physically resident at once. Blocks are admitted onto SMs as registers, shared memory, thread limits, warp limits and block limits allow. Even after a warp becomes resident, it may still be waiting on memory, an arithmetic dependency or synchronization. The scheduler can only choose from warps that are actually eligible to issue.

That changed how I read performance numbers too.

Occupancy is a residency number => resident warps compared with the architectural maximum. GPU utilization measures something different. In NVML it is basically the fraction of the sampling window during which at least one kernel was executing.

So a GPU can show 100% utilization without Tensor Cores being saturated, without HBM bandwidth being saturated, and while one subsystem is the bottleneck and large parts of the GPU remain underused.

Memory has the same kind of traps. Registers, shared memory, L1, L2 and HBM are not just increasingly slower boxes. They have different scope, capacity, management and access behavior.

A model fitting in HBM tells you that it fits. It tells you almost nothing about how many bytes move, whether accesses coalesce well, how much reuse you get, or whether memory is what is holding the kernel back.

FlashAttention is a nice example => the dense attention math stays the same, but the execution schedule is reorganized to reduce traffic between HBM and on-chip storage.

Tensor Cores were another thing I had mentally oversimplified. They are specialized matrix multiply-accumulate hardware and they matter enormously for AI, but they do not “run the model.” Reductions, indexing, elementwise work, synchronization, memory movement, launches and plenty of other instructions still go through other parts of the GPU.

After a while I stopped asking "why isn’t the GPU at 100%?" and started asking a better question => what is actually limiting useful progress right now?

That ended up becoming a 42-page handbook.

SMs, warps, schedulers, occupancy, latency hiding, registers, shared memory, caches, HBM, coalescing, Tensor Cores, GEMM mapping, precision, utilization and the performance numbers that are very easy to misread.

Some time ago I wrote about a publication (https://lnkd.in/dAhQuh3r) that vividly described how AI would soon not just transform work, but wipe out entire job categories within a few years. It illustrated the transformation of economic structures, mass unemployment across entire industries, and riots against AI companies.

Interestingly, the AI apocalypse has been somewhat delayed for a single reason: the attempt to model human thinking was TOO successful. Neural networks successfully mimic humans — not just in their virtues but in their flaws: they chase their own metrics, miss context, take unsolicited and unnecessary initiative, or — conversely — act incredibly dense, running in circles while "pondering."

Ultimately, they deceive, too.

And since they do everything a thousand times faster and more meticulously than a human, their deceptions are far more convincing — it’s nearly impossible to catch them out. While you can often tell from a person's face whether they are lying or simply honestly mistaken, that distinction doesn't exist with AI. A neural network can use a convincing tone to make you sure of absolutely anything — until you actually verify the facts.

Consequently, all attempts to entrust them with serious, multi-faceted tasks have so far proven unsuccessful. We are still a long way off from the scenario where an AI becomes the CEO of a real company (you may remember the taxi service from Cyberpunk 2077). A setup involving countless agents working together and cross-checking one another seems like a viable option, but it is extremely expensive and requires highly customized configuration.

Incidentally, companies — and individuals in their private lives — spend a vast amount of time and money trying to verify whether a specific person and their words can be trusted, which shows how central trust already is.

I wonder whether AI itself will eventually solve this problem.

That’s probably how an AI would start this post if I asked it to.

“The question is no longer whether we like artificial intelligence-generated content; we use it every day. The question is — why do we hate it?”
That’s what the AI ​​would ask.

And I would answer like this:
• We know what’s coming next, so we get bored. It’s like the three chords in basic pop music. Sure, there are masterpieces in that genre, but mostly it’s incredibly dull — you can predict every single note.
• We follow people because of their unique backgrounds and experiences. We don’t need generic truisms; we want to learn the secret of success from someone who has actually achieved it. We want to feel the emotions of someone who has actually lived through them. We can generate the rest ourselves.
• There’s a related point: we don’t like being deceived. If you’re using AI to write, just say so. Why pretend to be someone you’re not?
• A specific breed of deceiver is the kind that’s after your money. Their posts usually start like this: “I’ve seen this in many companies.” Or: “Clients often come to me with this request.” There’s nothing to add here; it borders on fraud. It’s like putting on a uniform and impersonating an on-duty police officer.

Until mandatory labeling for AI-generated text becomes the norm, tell me: how do you spot “neuro-slop”? Based on what criteria?

Everyone is chasing AGI. But what if the concept itself is the problem?

A recent paper by Goldfeder, Wyder, Yann LeCun and Shwartz-Ziv (Columbia, Distyl, NYU) argues exactly that. Their core claim: human intelligence isn't general, it's specialised by evolution. We're only good at tasks that were critical for our survival. Everything else, we're mediocre at best.

The paper makes the No Free Lunch argument: with finite compute, a system concentrating capability on a narrower task domain will always outperform a system spreading that compute across everything. This is the mathematical foundation for why a clinical specific AI Twin will outperform GPT-N at clinical reasoning, and why a legal AI Twin will outperform it at regulatory interpretation.

Their proposed replacement: Superhuman Adaptable Intelligence (SAI), intelligence measured not by how many tasks it can perform, but by how fast it can adapt to exceed humans at any important task.

The key insight from the paper that stuck with me: "The AI that folds our proteins should not be the AI that folds our laundry."

This validates something we've been building toward at Qiri.

SAI gives you the theory. It tells you why specialization wins. But it leaves an open question: what does a specialized, adaptable system actually look like when deployed inside a real professional domain, pharmacy, law, engineering, finance?

That's the gap we're working in. We call it Domain AGI.

Where SAI says "measure adaptation speed," Domain AGI asks: how fast can a pharmacy AI Twin adapt to a new drug class, a regulatory update, a patient edge case that sits outside the training data?

Where SAI says "embrace specialisation," Domain AGI defines what specialisation actually means at the role level, the knowledge architecture, the reasoning patterns, the safety boundaries, the governance layer that determines what the AI knows, how it reasons, and where it stops.

Where SAI rejects human-level benchmarks as the goal, Domain AGI sets a higher bar: not matching the average practitioner, but matching the best practitioners at their best, and then scaling that judgment to every workstation, every shift, every patient.

SAI is the physics. Domain AGI is the engineering.

If you're building in this space, specialist intelligence scoped to a professional domain; I'd love to hear how you're thinking about it.

Gartner says 90% of all B2B purchases will be handled by AI agents by 2028. That's $15 trillion in spending flowing through automated exchanges. Not someday. In three years.

And most businesses are completely unprepared for it.
Not in a sci-fi way. In a very boring, practical, already-happening way.

AI agents are starting to make real procurement decisions. Evaluating vendors. Comparing contracts. Initiating purchases. And most businesses are completely unprepared for it.

I asked someone running sales at a mid-sized SaaS company what happens when the person on the other side of their next deal isn't a person.
They laughed. Then went quiet.

Your landing page, your SDR sequence, your brand story, none of it was built for a buyer that doesn't feel, doesn't get impressed, and can cross-reference 47 vendors in three seconds.

Here's the part most people miss.
"The AI agents doing the buying won't be generic. The good ones will be Digital Twins/Companion built on specific human experts. A CFO Twin doesn't just evaluate cost. It evaluates cost the way that CFO evaluates cost, shaped by their risk appetite, their past mistakes, their institutional memory."

This isn't a bot. This is encoded human judgment making consequential decisions at scale.

I called to ask the price of one ticket to Antarctica. I got off the phone having put a $50,000 deposit on the entire ship.

2015. 106 people, ten days, the bottom of the world.

116.

What if I bought the whole boat?

A year later I'd filled it — largely by cold-calling entrepreneurs I had never met and opening with "Hi, I'm Julio, do you want to go to Antarctica?" We spent ten days future-pacing: what are we pretending not to know, about business, about people, about the country we'd all just flown away from.

On day six I asked the captain whether we could swim. Minus two degrees, liquid only because it's salt water. He opened the side of the ship and we broke the record that day for passengers entering the water off one boat.

None of it required capital I didn't have or courage I didn't have. It required one more question than the conversation was asking for. Most opportunities die at exactly that point — the moment where it would be slightly awkward to keep going.

If you're in a negotiation this week and you've already decided where you'll stop asking — that stopping point is the price you're paying.

Ask the last question.

Buy your own home and you pay for it. Alone. Nobody is coming to help. Hold property as an investment and the structure changes — there's a tenant, and there's the tax treatment. Same word on the loan document. Completely different exposure.

That Christmas conversation is where JDL Strategies started. Just Do Life.

I'm not telling anyone to go and borrow a million dollars. Leverage magnifies outcomes in both directions, the numbers only work under specific conditions, and every situation is genuinely different — that's a conversation for your accountant, not a LinkedIn post.

Connecting AI to your tools is a starting point. But it doesn’t automatically give your teams the knowledge they need. That knowledge can still be scattered across people and systems, or mixed with conversations that shouldn’t be shared broadly.
 
The challenge isn’t simply giving AI more access. It’s making useful knowledge available to the right people, with the right restrictions.
 
BackEngine brings customer emails, calls, messages, and account information together into organized knowledge your teams can use in their existing AI tools.
 
Your company controls which customer accounts each person can access, whether they can receive insights or underlying sources, and which sensitivity levels they may access. BackEngine classifies each interaction by sensitivity to support those controls.

Claude is becoming the next work OS.

Not a great LLM. Not a chatbot. The place where work happens.

Microsoft Office owned the workday for 30 years (with Google Workspace making progress). But work is moving to Claude, fast.

Email is already there (Gmail, Superhuman MCPs). Research is there (Deep Research). Dashboards are there (Live Artifacts). Scheduled automations are there (Co-Work Scheduled). Your data is there. Most of mine already is.

This was my morning.

I got to the office. Opened up Claude. Inside was a TLDR on all the emails and slacks I had missed with drafted responses to any that required it. I sent 8 of them.

A few minutes later I got a list of all the people that had visited BackEngine that matched our ICP, with their email address pulled up and a draft ready to go.  I sent them. 

I then opened up a Live Artifact in Claude that showed me what we had shipped in the past week, what tickets were being worked on, and what was not being worked on. 

I then got a summary of everything we had spent money on the past 7 days. One item looked like a billing mistake. I slacked the team to find out if it was real or not.

I then had a case study interview with a customer. As soon as it was done, I asked Claude to find our other case studies and to write a similar one based on the transcript. 

And then I asked Claude to summarize the morning and write this post.

A couple of takeaways.

1) Building a horizontal productivity tool in 2026 is a fool's errand. No one is going to leave Claude to use your standalone dashboard, your standalone inbox, your standalone CRM UI. 
2) What's worth building: things Claude won't, that live inside Claude.

I am fascinated by the answers I get to this question. No two answers have been the same. 

Some have Copilot and called it done.

A bunch have a few random tools and a Slack channel where people paste prompts at each other.

Then I ask about the change management. How do they get people to use it and adopt new habits.

Lunch and learns. Certification tracks. Internal prompt libraries nobody opens. Champion programs. Most are not really doing much and letting it sorts itself out.

I am not really surprised. It is all happening so fast. 

We are very clearly still in the invent-your-own-thing phase. No one has really figured out best practices. And even if they had, it would be obsolete in 3 days anyway.

- if you are serious about transforming your team with AI. Make sure you have a single-threaded leader with actual authority to make it happen.

"Implemented" is four different things, and the difference costs about six months.

 Built. Tested on site. Accepted into trial operation. Running in production. On a slide, all four get the same word —
 implemented.

 🏭 The gap shows up later. A system that was "implemented" turns out to be a demo stand assembled in three weeks. The
 pilot that "went live" ran on one object, with one crew, in good weather. Nobody lied. The word just did too much
 work.

 ⚙️ The question that separates them takes one sentence: which stage is your system in at your current clients — name
 the stage, the object, and the date. A strong answer splits it up on its own: here we're running trials, here it's
 trial operation, here it's production, and here are the limits. A weak answer repeats the word.

 📋 We put this into a checklist for technical buyers choosing an industrial ERP or HSE contractor in Kazakhstan. 25
 questions. It contains no vendor comparison and no "correct" answers — on some of them, a strong contractor will have
 to say no. We suggest asking them to everyone in the selection, including us.

 Which stage is the system you're being sold actually in?

🔒 What "Safety-First" Actually Means — And Why Most Companies Get It Wrong
Everyone in oil & gas, maritime, and heavy industry says they're "safety-first."
But here's the uncomfortable truth:
If your Permit to Work system runs on paper, carbon copies, and signatures nobody reads — you don't have a safety culture. You have a compliance ritual.
Safety-first isn't a slogan on a wall. It's a system where: → Every worker knows exactly what hazards exist before they start → Every permit is traceable, timestamped, and accountable → Every violation triggers a response — not next week, right now → Every near-miss becomes data, not a forgotten conversation
Paper can't do this. Paper gets lost, backdated, signed in bulk, filed and forgotten.
Software doesn't replace safety culture — it makes it enforceable.
When a PTW system goes digital:
A permit can't be "approved" without verified checklist completion
Expiry is automatic — no more workers operating on yesterday's permit
Management sees real-time dashboards, not monthly reports
Incident patterns become visible before they become fatalities
The shift isn't from paper to screen. It's from intention to infrastructure.
Safety-first means building systems where cutting corners is harder than doing it right.
That's what we build at Jana-System Digital.
This is Post 2 of a series on why digitization in safety-critical industries isn't optional — it's overdue.

Paper permits are still the standard in industrial safety.

Fill out the form. Get five signatures. File it in a cabinet. Hope nobody loses it.

We decided to change that.

At Jana System Digital, we built PTW System — a digital Permit-to-Work platform that replaces the entire paper workflow. Android, iOS, and a web-based admin panel.

Here's how verification works: every permit approval is confirmed with the device's IMEI and a photo of the signatory. No wet signatures. No ambiguity about who approved what, when, and where.

The system handles the full cycle — from permit creation and risk assessment to hazard catalogs, user roles, and real-time status tracking. All in three languages: Russian, Kazakh, and English.

This week, we officially entered the Pilot Industrial Testing phase with a company specializing in emergency spill response on water — an environment where safety protocols aren't optional, they're critical.

This is a major milestone for our team. It means the product is no longer a prototype — it's being validated in a real operational environment, with real permits, real crews, and real hazardous conditions.

Sometimes the boldest ideas start with being completely broke.

In 2025, French entrepreneur Dagobert Renouf faced a classic dilemma: he wanted a meaningful wedding but couldn’t afford it. Instead of going into debt or scaling back, he did something unconventional.

He sold advertising space on his wedding tuxedo.

He posted the idea online, set clear pricing based on logo placement, and within weeks 26 startups said yes. Companies like Comp AI, Inbox Zero, FeatherFlow and others paid to have their logos embroidered on his suit. On his wedding day, he walked down the aisle as a walking billboard for the indie hacker community.

The result: Roughly $10,000 raised. After the custom suit and taxes, he walked away with a free tuxedo and about $2,000 in his pocket.

What I love about this story isn’t just the creativity, it’s the mindset.

Dagobert didn’t wait for perfect conditions. He didn’t ask for charity. He created a clear value exchange: visibility for the startups in exchange for support. He treated a personal milestone as a marketing opportunity without losing the joy of the day. And the community responded because the idea was bold, transparent, and fun.

In a world that often rewards playing it safe, this is a reminder:

Constraints can be the best catalysts for innovation.  
A simple, well-packaged ask can open doors you didn’t know existed.  
And sometimes the most memorable brand campaigns aren’t planned by agencies, they’re invented by people who simply refuse to stay stuck.

Spec-Driven Development is having a moment.

GitHub shipped spec-kit. OpenAI is pushing "natural language as the new programming language." Every AI tooling pitch is a variation of: write the spec, hand it to the model, get the code.

The framing is misleading.

Dave Farley has been telling you to do this for fifteen years. Dan North coined BDD in 2006. The point was always the same: write requirements in a form that is unambiguous and executable. Code is a byproduct of clearly stating what you want.

Most teams ignored it. Gherkin became ceremony. Cucumber became a graveyard. The discipline was right; the payoff was diffuse.
What changed isn't the philosophy. It's the economics.

BDD asked engineers to do extra work for a payoff they couldn't feel. LLMs punish vague specs in real time — hand a model an ambiguous spec, it confidently ships the wrong thing in twenty seconds. The feedback loop BDD always wanted finally exists, because imprecision now costs you visibly and immediately.

The rigor was always the point. AI just made the rigor pay.
Practical implication for founders hiring engineers: the people who can actually do SDD well are the people who could have done BDD well. They think in invariants. They write specs that exclude ambiguity. Give them Claude or Codex and they ship like a team of four.

Give the prompt-and-pray crowd the same tools and they ship technical debt at four times the rate.

The dominant narrative about AI and engineering teams:

"AI makes developers more productive. More productive developers means you need fewer. Smaller teams. Lower burn. Done."

I've watched founders act on this logic. Here's what usually happens instead.
They hire fewer engineers. They pick for availability over seniority — because the assumption is AI closes the gap. They ship fast for six to ten weeks. Then something breaks that the AI-assisted engineer doesn't know how to diagnose. 
Or a new hire joins and can't understand the codebase they've inherited. Or they need to scale a system built to demo, not to run.

AI didn't make the team more productive at that point. It made them faster at building the wrong thing.

Here's the mechanism nobody's talking about:
AI raised the ceiling on what a small team can attempt. So founders — reasonably — attempt more. The scope expands. The complexity expands. 

What's changed is who can write the first version. What hasn't changed is who needs to be responsible for the second, third, and tenth.
What you need less of: engineers doing mechanical work AI handles well. Scaffolding, boilerplate, CRUD.

What you need more of: senior engineers who govern what AI produces. Who know which decisions will hurt at scale. Who recognize when "it works" isn't the same as "you can build on it."

The 1-junior-plus-AI bet fails for a specific reason: AI fills in knowledge gaps with confident-sounding code that a junior engineer doesn't know to question.

The correct model: 1–2 senior AI-native engineers produce what a pre-AI team of 3–5 used to — at a standard you can actually build on.
"Force multipliers amplify what's already there. Make sure what's there is worth amplifying."

I’m seeing a lot of hype around the story of an AI agent deleting a database at RocketOS.
But to me, the bigger issue is not “AI went rogue.” 

It’s the same engineering failure we’ve seen for years: non-isolated backups, overly broad access rights, and weak guardrails around production systems.

Humans make this exact kind of mistake every day under the same conditions. The difference is that when AI does it, it becomes a headline.

The real takeaway is simple: good engineering practices matter even more now. Least privilege, environment isolation, approval flows, backup separation, and recovery planning are not optional when agents can take actions at machine speed.

If an agent can delete production data, the problem is not just the agent. The problem is the system design around it.
AI doesn’t remove the need for discipline. It raises the cost of not having it.

Bir CTO ajandasından;

Açıkçası böyle günlerde kutlama paylaşımları hazırlayan biri değilim. Genelde klavyeyi daha teknik işler için kullanıyorum. :)

Ama bugün, hayatımın büyük kısmını verdiğim sektör için birkaç satır yazmak notlarımda yazmayan bir görevim.

Fintech’te iş ortakları, üreticiler, müşteriler ve ekosistemin diğer üyeleri çoğunlukla, temas ettikleri son 1-2 saniyeyi konuşuyor.

- Başarılı ödemeler
- Hızlı işlemler
- Sorunsuz deneyimler

Biz ise o 1-2 saniye için bazen haftalarca aynı konu üzerinde çalışan, tartışan, deneyen ve en değerli kaynağımız olan zamanı harcayan kişileriz.

Bir yandan teknoloji, bir yandan ürün, bir yandan ekip, bir yandan şirket, bir yandan sektör, bir yandan iş ortakları.

Çünkü fintech’te en büyük başarı, iş ortaklarının, müşterilerin ve ekosistemin güvenini milisaniyeler içinde kazanırken, o güveni yıllar boyunca kesintisiz sürdürebilmektir.

CTO olmak ile girişimci olmak arasında düşündüğümden daha fazla ortak nokta varmış.

- Hiçbir gün birbirinin aynısı olmuyor.
- Biri diğerini kolaylaştırmıyor.

Aksine ikisi de birbirini sürekli zorluyor ve geliştiriyor. Ama galiba en güzel ortak özellikleri şu;

Ne zaman biri “biraz dinleneyim” dese, diğeri “tamam, şimdi sıra bende” diyerek devreye giriyor. Birbirlerinin resmen redundancy’si oluyorlar :)

Bu yolculukta hala her gün yeni şeyler öğreniyorum. Bazen saniyeler içinde, bazen geceleri birbirine bağlayan günlerde.

Ama öğrendiğim birkaç şey hiç değişmedi.

- İyi bir ekip kurmak zor.
- İyi bir kültür oluşturmak daha da zor.

Ama o kültür oluştuğunda, en zor problemler bile çözülemeyecek işler olmaktan çıkıyor.

Bunlara ek olarak;

Bir de girişimcinin, ihtiyaç duyduğunda fikrine danışabileceği, tecrübesinden faydalanabileceği büyüklerinin, arkadaşlarının ve iş ortaklarının olması gerçekten büyük bir şans. Ben bu konuda kendimi şanslı hissedenlerdenim.

Bugün vesilesiyle hem onlara hem de birlikte üreten ekip arkadaşlarıma teşekkür etmek istedim.

Dünya Fintech Günü kutlu olsun.

Üreten, geliştiren ve her gün o görünmeyen kısmı daha iyi hale getirmek için emek veren herkesin emeğine sağlık 🚀

Yapacak daha çok iş, üretilecek daha çok değer var.

Not: Kod yazmak, e-posta yazmak, hatta sözleşme maddesi hazırlamak, bunların hepsi bu paylaşımı yazmaktan daha kolaymış :)

I've always hated the saying "we're like family here" when it comes to work. Because it's obviously not true, and it's usually cynically invoked by management to entice an undue obligation of sacrifice. Implying that you should give it all to The Company -- constantly working weekends, always being available on vacations, and all the rest -- but when the necessities of the business change, you'll realize the obligation was never truly mutual.

But if work is not a family, what is it then?

I think Netflix got it right: it's a professional team. One where colleagues earn a spot by being really good in their given position. But also -- and this is the hard part! -- one where someone may fail to make the cut, if they aren't up to the standards of the team, don't fit in the given position, or simply hasn't been playing well enough for a while.

You can't have it both ways. You can't scorn the use of "we're a family" and then also expect that colleagues who can't keep up are spared the cut. It's either or, if you're going to have a high-performing team.

Think of it this way. There are probably thousands who play soccer at some level of professionalism. But there are only 11 spots on the starting lineup of Manchester United. You can be very good at soccer, and still not be part of that lineup.

Now the natural delusion of every business owner is to think that they're running Manchester United when in fact they're barely hanging on in third division. But the point is actually the same. Even in third division, there's a level of competence that makes someone a good fit. We can't all be the best. But there's room for almost anyone who's half-way decent to play (or work) productively SOMEWHERE.

And the reality is that if someone is a fit for third division, they'd have a terrible time at Manchester United. Expectations would be sky high. The gaps in their competency would quickly and painfully be revealed. They'd soon realize they're in the wrong place. Cutting them from the team would be an act of mercy, not cruelty.

Note that it's more than fine to give someone who shows promise a chance in a position that seems like a stretch. But after a couple of games, the progress should be apparent. Either you're revealing the fact that they're quickly stepping up to the role or you're revealing the fact that they won't.  

This is perhaps the most important job of the coach or manager. Knowing when to make the cut, and having the strength to do it. There'll always be a million reasons why you should wait longer, be more patient. But to do the job of being in charge well, you have to be decisive in face of incomplete evidence.

Not everyone is meant to be Messi or to play on his team. But we wouldn't have much of a sport if his level was the only level. Find your level, find a team that fits with it, and play to the best of your ability. That's the beautiful game.

Two predictions about AI in software development have hardened into conventional wisdom. Both are wrong.

The first says developers are obsolete. The second says software itself is obsolete.

Both confuse a demo with a product. And both miss the only resource that has ever mattered in this industry: time.

After two decades of building, leading engineering teams, and shipping products through every major platform shift since DHTML, here is the thesis:

AI will not make software free. It will make iteration cheap. The rest is consequence.

In the essay I work through:

- Why the output gap between juniors and seniors is narrowing, but the judgment gap is not
- The apprenticeship problem: we just automated the grind that used to produce seniors
- Why people will keep paying for software (you are not buying code, you are buying compressed refinement cycles plus someone to call when it breaks)
- How two week sprints compress to two or four days, and why teams shipping at the new cadence without upgrading their review and testing discipline are not shipping faster, they are shipping debt faster
- What tailoring software to individual users should and should not mean
- Why trust and explainability become the medium term bottleneck
