En ofattbar och surrealistisk känsla infinner sig.

Vår älskade Måns lämnade jordelivet i helgen. Mindre än en vecka efter vårt sista telefonsamtal. Vi hann aldrig ses i Torsdags.. 

Kampen mot cancern blev till slut för svår. Men jag vet att han kämpade med full kraft. Får sån var Måns. En kämpe som alltid krigade in i det sista.

I över 15 år tog vi oss igenom otaliga nattpass sida vid sida och det skapades några av de mest episka minnena som man nu bär med sig resten av livet. Tillsammans upplevde vi blod, svett och tårar men också massvis med fantastiska stunder präglade av humor av den mest speciella sorten (ni som vet ni vet). 

Måns fick oss alla att skratta. Han fick människor att känna sig inkluderade och välkomna samtidigt som han ingav ett lugn och en känsla av trygghet för såväl kunder som för kollegor. Måns hade alltid din rygg. 

Ett starkt minne var när jag blev påhoppad med en flaska i bakhuvudet. Då var Måns den första att komma till undsättning även om han själv utsatte sig för fara och faktiskt blev skadad på kuppen. Men sån var Måns. Någon man alltid kunde lita på och som inte skulle tveka en sekund att ställa upp när det väl gällde. En brother in arms.

Jag finner inga vettiga ord att beskriva den tomhet och saknad jag känner för min broder.

Men legenden lever vidare. Alltid saknad. Aldrig glömd.

Måns Månsson 1974-2026 🕊️

😥  Somewhere in your “My Courses” tab, there is probably a course you started with real motivation and quietly abandoned around lesson nine. 😥 

I don’t think that means you’re lazy.

🧩 I think it means the format is broken. 

📺 Most online courses are built like broadcasts. 

Someone records a sequence once, for an imagined average student, and then the same path plays back for everyone.

That creates a few problems:
👉 The course keeps moving when you’re stuck.
👉 Lesson seven assumes lesson six fully landed. But if you half-understood one concept, the gap compounds. By lesson ten, the subject feels impossible, not because it is impossible, but because it’s sitting on a floor with a hole in it.
👉 The course mistakes watching for learning.
👉 The progress bar fills because the video played, not because anything actually clicked. You can “complete” a module and still be unable to explain or apply the thing it taught.
👉 The course forgets your weak spots.

🟢 The concepts you missed should come back later, at the right moment. 

🔴 Instead, the syllabus marches forward and your confusion from week three never gets another look.

🧠 This hurts self-learners the most. 🧠 

In university, a static lecture comes wrapped in scaffolding: deadlines, problem sets, office hours, classmates, TAs.

A self-learner has none of that.

The recorded course is the whole system.

So when it cannot notice you’re stuck, change pace, ask better questions, or remember what you missed, the learner has to provide all the structure, feedback, and accountability themselves.

That’s exactly what they came to the course to get. 🙂

I don’t think the future is just “better videos.”

🚀 I think it’s learning paths that adapt: 🚀 
A sequence built for your level.
Practice in every section.
Feedback based on your actual answer.
Checkpoints that test mastery, not completion.
Memory across sessions, so tomorrow doesn’t start from zero.

🐒 That’s what we’re trying to build with Benji. 🐒 
Not a playlist.
Not a progress bar.
A learning loop that notices where you are and helps you keep going. 🧠

Yesterday’s massive AWS outage — caused by something as “simple” as a DNS resolution failure — took down major platforms worldwide: Fortnite, Snapchat, Alexa, and countless others.

This is a powerful reminder that resilience isn’t optional. Even the biggest, most redundant infrastructures fail — and when they do, the ripple effects are enormous.

💡 Designing for failure means assuming the worst will happen:
	•	Multi-region or multi-cloud architecture
	•	Graceful degradation when dependencies fail
	•	Health checks and failover testing, not just backups
	•	Clear incident playbooks and communication paths

The companies that stayed online yesterday weren’t lucky — they were prepared.

Resilience is not about preventing failure. It’s about surviving it.

Yeni Test Automation Framework layihəmi paylaşmaq istəyirəm!

 Gauge Framework ilə işləyib, UI və API testləri üçün genişləndirilə bilən bir arxitektura qurdum.

Cucumber vs Gauge - Fərqlər nədir?

Çoxları Cucumber ilə tanışdır, amma Gauge-i sınayandan sonra gördüm ki, bəzi hallarda daha güclü alternativdir:

Cucumber:
- Gherkin sintaksisi (Given-When-Then)
- Geniş community dəstəyi
- Step Definition-lar arasında code duplicate problemi yarana bilir
- Feature file strukturu daha sərt

Gauge:
- Markdown-based spec faylları (daha oxunaqlı)
- Concept-lər vasitəsilə step-ləri qruplaşdırmaq mümkün
- Refactoring daha asan (spec və kod eyni anda dəyişir)
- Paralel icra daha effektiv
- Data-driven testing üçün daha yaxşı dəstək

 Gauge-in üstünlükləri:
✅ Plugin arxitekturası - istədiyiniz reporting tool-u əlavə edə bilərsiniz
✅ IDE dəstəyi - IntelliJ və VS Code üçün əla pluginlər
✅ Konsept faylları - təkrarlanan step-ləri bir yerdə toplayıb istifadə edə bilərsiniz
✅ Specs-dən birbaşa kod refactor - spec faylını dəyişəndə Java kodu da avtomatik update olur

Layihədə istifadə etdiyim arxitektura:

 Helper Pattern:
- ApiHelper, ClickHelper, TypeHelper, VerifyHelper
- Hər helper öz funksionallığından məsulduр
- Code reusability maksimum səviyyədə

 Implementation Layer:
- Step-lər ayrı implementation class-larında
- Browser, API, Element əməliyyatları təmiz şəkildə ayrılıb
- Single Responsibility Principle

 Resource Management:
- JSON-based locator management (XPath-ləri kod içində saxlamaq yox)
- API body-lər ayrı JSON fayllarında
- Environment-specific konfiqurasiyalar

 Bu arxitekturanın üstünlükləri:

1 Genişləndirilə bilir - yeni helper və ya implementation əlavə etmək asandır
2 Maintain edilməsi rahat - locator dəyişəndə yalnız JSON faylını update edirsən
3 Test data-nı kod-dan ayırır - API body-lər, locator-lar hamısı ayrıca
4 Yeni proyektə uyğunlaşdırmaq asan - sadəcə spec və locator fayllarını dəyişirsən
5 Komanda üçün oxunaqlı - Spec faylları texniki bilməyən adamlar da başa düşür

 Texnologiyalar:
- Java 11
- Gauge Framework
- Selenium WebDriver 4.28
- REST Assured
- Maven
- WebDriverManager

#tldr
AI makes us feel incredibly #fast because it hides the #foundation of our work. When you don't build the #implementation yourself, you lose the #context - leading to a hidden cycle of endless automated #rework.

From engineering to marketing and sales, everyone feels like they are moving at lightning speed because AI can spit out a finished product in seconds.

But curiously, final project timelines aren't actually shrinking.

​I think it comes down to a loss of context.
​When you do a task manually, you’re forced to wrestle with the ugly, foundational stuff. You are constantly thinking about the database structure, the security measures, the compliance rules, or the core brand guidelines.

Because you touch every piece of the architecture, you naturally catch structural flaws before they happen.

​When you hand that implementation over to an AI, those foundations become invisible to you.
​The AI gives you a beautifully polished result, but it makes assumptions about your system or your logic that you didn't see. The draft looks perfect, so you feel fast. But because you skipped the foundational thinking, those hidden flaws don't surface until you hit testing or launch.

​And here’s the trap: because you didn't write the original work, you don't fully understand it. So when it breaks, you deploy more AI to try and patch the errors. Suddenly, you're stuck in an endless loop of automated rework, and your overall timeline stretches right back to where it used to be.

Manual work forces you to prevent mistakes; AI work forces you to hunt them down after the fact.

​The only way I've seen to mitigate this is to change how we use the tools. We have to stop treating AI as a shortcut to bypass the thinking. If we don’t spend the time defining the strict boundaries, the structures, and the rules before the machine generates the output, we’re just trading five minutes of writing for five hours of managing a mess.… more

For a #developer today, a significant chunk of time can be spent on the architecture surrounding the #AI #configuration rather than the code itself.

We’ve reached a point where #LLMOps (LLM Operations) is a full-time discipline, and it’s mostly focused on managing the "efficiency tax" of intelligence.

The shift toward efficiency engineering involves a few critical levers:

Smart #Routing: Not every task requires a frontier model. Logic can be built to route basic requests to smaller, cheaper models, saving the "heavy lifting" for where it actually adds value.

Semantic #Caching: If a system pays to generate the same response twice, that’s a margin leak. Implementing a layer that recognizes and retrieves similar intents is often the difference between a profitable feature and a budget drain.

#Token Management: In 2026, "lean context" is the new "clean code." Every unnecessary token is a cost. Curating exactly what goes into the prompt and what stays out, is a core part of the development cycle.

The #differentiator isn't just having access to AI. It's the #infrastructure that makes it sustainable. If a team is spending more time on routing, caching, and cost-control than on the prompts themselves, it’s not a distraction - it’s the job.

I was VP of Engineering at Goldman Sachs. 
The hardest part of leaving it and starting a startup wasn't the money. 

It was breaking the habits and deprogramming myself.

At big companies, you don't just do things. You check with people first. You get everyone to agree. You wait for the right meeting. For 10 years, I did that without thinking about it.

Then you're at a startup with no one to align with and nothing to wait for, and none of it works anymore.

So I had to unlearn it.

A thing that did surprise me was I thought moving fast meant being messy or unorganized, It doesn't. I'm still an organized person. That never changed. I just stopped organizing everything before I start. Now I start, and I build the structure as I go.

Both gears at once.

And that's what i look for when i hire. Not the perfect resume. Someone who can hold structure and speed at the same time and doesn't wait for permission to start. We're hiring engineers like that right now.

"AI-native" has become a sticker people slap on a normal company. A copilot here, an automation there, a brokerage with agents bolted on the side.

Wrong model.

At Harper it means something almost uncomfortable: the company itself is the product.

Dakotah Rice wrote about "operating memory", the idea that AI can't replace tribal knowledge until it's been captured. Once you capture that, the exception, the workaround, the underwriter who'll touch a hard-to-place risk, the company stops being people using tools and becomes a system an intelligence runs. We're rebuilding commercial insurance this way, intake, submissions, quoting, servicing, renewals, making every step computational instead of manual.

Jack Dorsey calls this building the company as an intelligence - AI at the center, people at the edge, a circle instead of a pyramid. He talks about a "world model" of your operations, a living record of every decision and process that gets deeper every time. That's operating memory at company scale.

And here's where the moat actually sits. Not in the agents. Agents help, but they're only as good as you align and shape them, and the taste, the pace, the thousand small nuances of how this company actually runs have to be curated by the operators who live in it. The agents are the medium, the hands that take the actions a human used to take. The moat is everything underneath: the intelligence, the knowledge, the processes, and the encoding of all of it into a substrate agents can run on. They don't create that judgment. People do.

Which is why this was never humans versus AI. The contrarian thing we learned is that you need more people than you'd expect, just doing different work. We don't remove humans, we reduce human time and change what that time is spent on. Agents take the action. People weave through the whole system: guiding what context gets captured, validating what the AI gets wrong, turning every correction into a label, a policy, a skill the agents learn from. The system captures. People shape and teach it. The job stops being "do the task" and becomes "own the outcome and improve the loop."

The models are good and getting better, even in narrow verticals. So the edge was never the model, and it was never the agents. It's the company underneath them. Whoever encodes their judgment fastest wins.

That's the services company of the future. We're building it, and hiring for everything.

I think AI systems will get cheaper not just because models get cheaper, but because we’ll get much better at knowing when expensive intelligence is actually necessary.

The smartest model isn’t the one you use everywhere.

It’s the one you use at the right moment.

The first thing I tell people building agents: 𝘂𝘀𝗲 𝗹𝗲𝘀𝘀 𝗶𝗻𝗳𝗿𝗮𝘀𝘁𝗿𝘂𝗰𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗲.

𝗗𝗼𝗻’𝘁 𝘀𝘁𝗮𝗿𝘁 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵: LangChain, LlamaIndex, CrewAI, multiple agents, and a complicated orchestration layer.

𝗦𝘁𝗮𝗿𝘁 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵: a good model, the right context, a simple data store, and one clear task.

I like to start really simple and understand how the model behaves. You don't need all of the orchestration on day one.

Once you start experimenting, you see what the system actually needs. You can go from one-step reasoning and one action to multi-step reasoning, and eventually to specialized agents for specific tasks.

Start simple, see how it behaves, and add complexity as you need it.

Complexity should be a response to failure, not a starting point.

- Being the one who understands all of it.

I've learned that successful leadership looks like:

I give my team a lot of freedom to make choices and decisions. Then we make sure we align in the direction. That part is very important. Velocity requires direction, not just speed.

2. Letting people make mistakes

I want independent operators with high agency. So I need to let them fail in a safe environment. 

3. Saying the hard things

I don't hide my thoughts as much anymore. In a culture which requires a lot of intensity, it's very good to be open and have a really high level of candor.

4. Changing your style as the company changes

I always wanted to manage people how I wanted somebody to manage me. I learned quickly that is not the right way to do it, because I'm a unique person. The style has to come from the season the company is in.

None of this comes naturally. Some weeks are hard.

LinkedIn almacena bastante información sobre nuestra red, pero la mayor parte está en texto libre.

Eso hace que responder preguntas sencillas no sea tan sencillo:

- ¿Qué industrias predominan?
- ¿Cuál es el nivel de seniority de mis contactos?
- ¿Qué porcentaje corresponde a perfiles técnicos, founders o ejecutivos?

Para responderlas desarrollé un pipeline que procesa un export de LinkedIn.

El flujo consiste en:

- Cargar y limpiar el archivo Connections.csv.
- Normalizar títulos de puestos escritos de distintas formas.
- Enriquecer cada registro mediante un LLM con atributos como industry, seniority, functional area, likely interests y otros.
- Agrupar los resultados para obtener una caracterización de la red.

Uno de los aprendizajes más interesantes fue comprobar cuánto influye el diseño del prompt en la clasificación. Un prompt con demasiado contexto puede introducir sesgos, por lo que opté por instrucciones lo más neutrales posible.

También ejecuté el procesamiento localmente con Ollama para mantener los datos fuera de servicios externos.

Más que el resultado puntual, lo valioso es contar con un proceso reproducible que permita volver a analizar la red cada vez que cambie.

Anthropic acaba de lanzar Claude Fable 5, y hay detalles que vale la pena entender si estás construyendo sobre estos modelos, o si simplemente te interesa saber a hacia dónde va la IA.

Algunas cosas que me llamaron la atención:

→ Es un modelo de clase "Mythos", un nivel por encima de Opus. Está a la vanguardia en casi todos los benchmarks conocidos, y la diferencia se amplía cuanto más larga y compleja es la tarea. Stripe reportó que hizo una migración completa en un codebase de 50 millones de líneas de Ruby en un día — algo que hubiera tomado a un equipo completo más de dos meses. Me hago la pregunta: ¿cómo va a cambiar esto el día a día del desarrollo de software?

→ Nuevas medidas de salvaguardas. Cuando una solicitud toca ciberseguridad, bio/quím o extracción de capacidades del modelo, en vez de negarse simplemente dirige el procesamiento a Opus 4.8, automáticamente. Los clasificadores están calibrados de forma conservadora — se activan en menos del 5% de las sesiones. Esto es relevante especialmente por mi trabajo en fintech e identidad, donde estás herramientas se perciben como nuevos riesgos de ciberseguridad. Es importante medir el uso del modelo con estas capacidades en ciberseguridad en actividades maliciosas.

→ El aspecto de ciberseguridad es tomado en serio. Se reporta que Mythos 5 tiene las mayores capacidades ofensivas de cualquier modelo en el mundo, y por eso está restringido a Project Glasswing. Al existir este modelo genera una dualidad donde lo mismo que ayuda a un defensor puede ayudar a un atacante — y al parecer Anthropic lo está tratando como un problema de primer nivel limitando el uso para esos aspectos.

→ Precio: $10 por millón de tokens de entrada, $50 de salida. Menos de la mitad que Mythos Preview. Y el doble que Claude Opus 4.8. Lo convierte en un modelo para utilizar en tareas especiales o presupuestar el costo vs el beneficio en tareas largas y complejas.

Lo que noto en esta nueva versión es mayor capacidad y salvaguardas en conjunto, así lo veremos mientras se evalúa su impacto. Para quienes tomamos decisiones de seguridad, compliance e infraestructura, eso es lo que hay que estudiar — no solo los scores en benchmarks.

¿Qué opinan del enfoque de Anthropic en crear un salvaguarda de respuesta al caer a un modelo distinto en vez de simplemente negarse a procesar?

1. La IA como herramienta de ataque
Sí, se menciona el uso de modelos como Claude y GPT 4.1 con ciertos prompts.
Pero la IA no ejecuta ataques por sí sola. Solo amplifica las capacidades del atacante.

2. Protección de datos en instituciones públicas
Cuando instituciones concentran grandes volúmenes de información sensible, el nivel de madurez en control de accesos, segmentación y monitoreo debe ser proporcional al riesgo.

3. Resiliencia de sistemas
La pregunta no es si habrá intentos de ataque.
Es qué tan rápido detectas, contienes y recuperas.

La resiliencia se demuestra en ejecución con:
– Protección de infraestructura crítica
– Gobernanza y gestión de riesgos
– Sistemas con Zero Trust
– Encriptación de datos
– Monitoreo continuo
– Respuesta coordinada

Entonces culpar a una herramienta puede generar titulares atractivos.
Pero no fortalece la resilencia.

La pregunta importante no es ¿La IA puede ser usada para atacar?
Eso ya es evidente.

La pregunta es:

Our vision outgrew our name.

Upkeep Care, the company founded with the vision of improving how social services reach people, is officially being renamed Keeper Systems.

Naming a company is surprisingly hard. You care so deeply about it, but at the beginning, you don’t fully know what the company will become. So how do you choose a name that reflects where you are today while leaving room for where you’re going?

Some close friends gave me honest feedback early on: “Upkeep” sounded like a cleaning service. They weren’t wrong. I grew up around my family’s dry cleaning business, so there was something nostalgic about it that I liked. But we knew it wasn’t quite right.

Keeper Systems represents the bolder future we have come to believe is possible through our work.

A future where connecting people to help is so efficient it actually saves money. In that future, when a government or community deploys a resource and someone qualifies for help, they receive it in seconds. Not months. Not never.

Nobody has done more with less than the people and organizations who have kept our social safety net afloat. We are building them the technology they deserve to turn this future into a reality.

The fear I hear most often about bringing AI into social services is that it will depersonalize the process and put vulnerable populations further at risk.

It's a fair concern. But I find myself asking a different question: how personalized and safe is the current process of accessing social services today?

Individuals in urgent need sit on hold for hours. Older adults are expected to navigate densely packed text on government websites. People in crisis are asked to complete multi-step administrative processes before they receive any help. Administrative capacity has quietly become a prerequisite for access.

The people who struggle the most have the least bandwidth to jump through these hoops. The current system isn't set up to serve them, not because it's inhumane, but because it's inefficient.

Every year, $140 billion in available government resources never reaches the people it was set aside to help. And every time a transformative technology emerges, it's the same communities that get left behind.

If AI can simplify complexity, shorten wait times, and guide people to the right support faster, it doesn't replace humanity - it makes space for it.

Our team at Upkeep Care is dedicating our lives to building the safest public-facing AI tools for connecting people to social services. Efficiency is the path to equity.

Thank you, Yale Institute for Global Health SHI, for bringing this to the top of mind. Always happy to be challenged and hear others' opinions and concerns!… more

🧐 Can ChatGPT prepare the Annual Financial report?
Now in Latvia it’s yearly report season for companies.

Well, yes, it can! At least till some point 

But you have to be ready to feed in a lot of information, so it’s much safer to do it in a private environment or private AI setup.

It also tends to get stuck in free-tier limitations, so it’s better to work in small steps.

And in the end, you still need to understand what you are doing. You need the wider picture — collisions, inconsistencies, risk points, accounting logic. AI can sometimes decide that a mismatch of €80 between debit and credit “is not a big issue” or “not resource efficient to solve.” That’s where human judgement still matters.

But with proper guidance, smart prompting, and real knowledge, AI becomes a very strong assistant. Especially in analytical work.

Honestly, I used to think accounting would be one of the last professions to be meaningfully assisted by AI.
Now I think it is already happening.

Not replacing professionals.
But significantly amplifying them.

I built ሃገራዊ (Hagerawi), a prediction market, because I kept thinking about three problems.

🔹The first problem is transparency and money flow.
In December 2025, Ethiopia revoked the licenses of all sports-betting organizations after a nationwide investigation into the sector. Authorities found that operators had paid only a fraction of the commission they owed and that large sums were moving outside the Government view. But demand did not disappear; it went underground. 𝗙𝗮𝗻𝗮 𝗠𝗲𝗱𝗶𝗮 𝗖𝗼𝗿𝗽𝗼𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻, a state-owned mass media outlet, now reports unlicensed betting transactions at around ETB 20 billion in September 2026 alone, with no tax collected, no reliable age checks, and no consumer protection. So instead of thinking only about banning the activity, I started thinking:

🔹What would a more transparent system look like?
Hagerawi (ሃገራዊ) is built around that question. It is a prediction market with payment integration using Telebirr in this project, through a sandbox environment, so transactions can be connected to a traceable digital payment system.

🔹The second problem is underage access.
One of the things that concerned me was minors and students getting access to betting platforms and developing unhealthy betting habits.
So I didn't want age verification to simply be a checkbox saying “I am 18+.”
I integrated the Fayda National ID concept into the system, using its sandbox APIs for the prototype, to explore how identity and age verification could happen before someone gets access to these features.

🔹The third problem is information.
This one goes beyond the prediction market.
We live in a world where people constantly make decisions based on information about the economy, policies, sports, and what might happen next.
But I kept asking myself:

🔹What if people could interact with information instead of just consuming it?
What if people could make predictions, see how other people think, discuss events, trade their views, and watch those collective expectations change over time? That idea became the foundation of ሃገራዊ.

PttAVM alışveriş deneyimim maalesef tam bir hayal kırıklığı oldu.
22 Haziran 2026 tarihinde PTTAVM üzerinden bir ürün sipariş ettim. Ürün ancak 2 Temmuz 2026 tarihinde tarafıma ulaştı. Aynı gün yetkili servisi arayarak kurulum talebinde bulundum ve servis 3 Temmuz'da kurulum için geldi.
Servis incelemesinde ürünün hasarlı olduğu tespit edildi ve değişim veya iade sürecinin başlatılması gerektiği belirtildi. Bunun üzerine servis tarafından resmi hasar tutanağı düzenlendi.
Aynı gün PTTAVM ile iletişime geçerek destek talebi oluşturdum. O tarihten bugüne kadar neredeyse her gün müşteri hizmetlerini aradım. Her görüşmede "konu acil olarak ilgili birime iletildi, en kısa sürede dönüş yapılacak" cevabını aldım. Ancak herhangi bir somut ilerleme sağlanmadı.
9 Temmuz 2026 tarihinde yaptığım görüşmede ses kaydı aldığımı ve gerekli olması halinde yasal haklarımı kullanacağımı belirttim. Buna rağmen süreç yine ilerlemedi.
Bugün, 14 Temmuz 2026 tarihinde tarafıma dönüş yapılarak sürecin ilerletileceği ve satıcı firma ile iletişime geçildiği söylendi. Oysa satıcı firma ile iletişime geçen ve süreci ilerletmeye çalışan kişi başından beri benim. Çünkü PTTAVM'den herhangi bir sonuç alamadığım için firmayla doğrudan görüşmek zorunda kaldım.
Ürünü teslim alalı 12 gün, hasar kaydı oluşturulalı 11 gün olmasına rağmen hâlâ net bir çözüm sunulmuş değil.
Amacım kimseyi karalamak değil. Ancak benzer alışveriş yapmayı düşünen insanların satış sonrası destek ve müşteri memnuniyeti konusunda yaşanabilecek sorunları bilmesini istiyorum.

Ayer vimos una consecuencia de un fenómeno cultural que, en gran medida, habíamos naturalizado. Como suele ocurrir, muchas prácticas pasan desapercibidas hasta que generan un daño real.

No creo que el problema sea quién comunica, sino cómo se comunica. Cualquier persona con llegada al público sea periodista, conductor, streamer o influencer tiene la responsabilidad de verificar la información antes de difundirla, especialmente cuando involucra la salud, la integridad o la vida de alguien.

La velocidad parece haberse vuelto más importante que la precisión. La necesidad de llegar primero muchas veces termina desplazando la obligación de corroborar los hechos. Y cuando eso ocurre, las consecuencias no son abstractas: hay familias, personas y reputaciones que pueden verse afectadas por información falsa.

Por eso no se trata de señalar culpables ni de promover una cacería de brujas. Florencia Peña pidió disculpas y difícilmente haya actuado con la intención de causar daño. Juzgar intenciones suele ser mucho más fácil que comprender el contexto completo de una situación.

El 20 de mayo sale WordPress 7.0.

Y tiene, probablemente, uno de los cambios más interesantes del año en software.

No es un copilot.
No es un chatbot.
No son sugerencias en el editor.

Es algo más estructural:

Reorganizaron el core para que un agente pueda operar WordPress por su cuenta.

Antes, si querías exponer una funcionalidad:
→ tocabas functions.php
→ registrabas un endpoint en la REST API
→ y rezabas que ningún plugin te rompiera algo

Ahora el sistema:
→ declara qué sabe hacer
→ un agente lo descubre
→ lo entiende
→ y lo ejecuta

Sin que tengas que cablear nada.

Ejemplo concreto:
“Creá un post sobre el lanzamiento, optimizalo para SEO, programalo mañana 9am y avisale al equipo en Slack.”

Hoy eso implica:
webhooks, integraciones a medida, glue code, mantenimiento.
En WordPress 7.0, un agente lo puede resolver solo.

Y para los que construimos productos sobre plataformas, esto cambia la pregunta de fondo:
Antes: ¿qué puede hacer mi sistema?
Ahora: ¿puede un agente operarlo?

Porque si la respuesta es no, en poco tiempo vas a estar compitiendo contra productos que sí.

Y esa brecha no se cierra con un sprint.

Todavía no está 100% terminado.
Pero la dirección ya quedó clara.

Y no es solo WordPress.

Es hacia dónde se está moviendo el software.

Trigger on Anything - and we mean anything. ⚡

This is week 4 of our weekly Flomation deep dive series. Each week we pick one feature and get into the detail of what it does, how it works, and why it matters.

This week: triggers.

---

What is it?

A workflow is only as useful as what starts it. If your automation tool only supports a handful of trigger types, your processes end up shaped around the tool's limitations rather than how your business actually works.

Flomation flips that. If something happens, Flomation can react to it.

---

How it works in Flomation:

Triggers are the entry point of every flow. You pick what fires it, configure it, and everything downstream runs automatically.

Supported triggers include HTTP webhooks, cron schedules, Git commits, S3 object events, incoming emails, form submissions, and even QR code scans.

That last one isn't a gimmick. Scan a QR code, kick off a workflow. The use cases are genuinely interesting.

---

Real world example:

Your team uses QR codes on physical assets in a warehouse. A staff member scans one with their phone.

Flomation picks up the scan, logs the location and timestamp to your database, checks the asset's maintenance schedule, and if it's overdue, automatically raises a job ticket in your system and notifies the relevant manager on Slack.

One scan. Fully automated response.

---

Why it matters:

For developers - stop building custom listener infrastructure for every event source. Flomation handles the ingestion, you just build the logic.

For business teams - your workflows can start from real-world events, not just software ones. That changes what automation can actually do for your operations.

---

Next week we're getting into Secrets, Secured - PGP-encrypted secrets, per-environment variables, and RBAC. Your credentials, handled properly. Follow Flomation so you don't miss it.

About
Most teams are still asking whether AI can write their code. If you run a platform or an engineering org, especially a regulated one, the more useful question is what you let it change, and what has to be true before you let it.
 
That is the work I do. We did not arrive with the agents: we built the platforms first.
 
I build and run platforms where a bad change is not just an outage: critical infrastructure, energy, and regulated professional services. Auditability is not a nice-to-have there, and "the model decided" is not an acceptable answer to a regulator. That constraint is what makes agentic AI genuinely hard rather than a demo.
 
I am still in enterprise platform teams every week. Right now that means extending a mobility operator's Pulumi-based platform into agent-driven workflows: skills, agents, feedback loops, and MCP servers giving those agents scoped access to pipelines and infrastructure state. We built that platform and delivered it, their own teams run on it now, and we are still in delivery as it grows. So the agents go into something we know from the inside. We now iterate on the agents more than on the code.
 
With an energy utility we built the platform, migrated it to AWS and have operated it since. The same idea, applied there to the unglamorous parts:
 → Security-finding triage, so the false-positive flood never lands on an engineer
 → Infrastructure-change review, catching destructive operations before apply
 → Documentation generated from the running system, not maintained beside it
 
The other half is how the code gets written. Our principle is enforce, don't instruct: an agent asked nicely to follow your architecture will drift, so the standard has to be mechanical. Spec first, rules the agent cannot ignore, tests and types as constraints rather than afterthoughts, small diffs, review loops with more than one agent, and CI that fails when the standard is broken. An agent that can change something needs something that can say no. Infrastructure should stay deterministic. Agents are an extra set of tools: good at triage and the work nobody has capacity for, bad at anything you cannot verify.
 
We work as a small senior team alongside a client's own platform organisation. No delivery pyramid: the people in the conversation are the people who build.
 
If you are working out where agents belong in your delivery, and where they don't, I am always happy to compare notes.

A utility's compliance function told us no.

We wanted an agent to triage security findings against their Kubernetes cluster. The finding volume was large and most of it was noise landing on one engineer, so the case was easy to make. The answer was still no. No AI system was getting access to that cluster.

That no was the most useful thing that happened in the project.
Because the honest version of "give the agent access" is: hand a model credentials and hope. They were right to refuse, and we did not yet have a good answer.

So we built one. A deterministic control layer between the agent and the system:
→ A defined tool set. The agent calls tools, never the cluster. Credentials are never handed to a model.
 → Every call logged. Not for us. For whoever has to review it afterwards.
 → Human approval before anything reaches production.
 → Policy enforced mechanically, not requested politely.

The agent stayed useful. The control point stayed auditable.

The general version, which I think is most of the game in regulated environments: an agent that can change something needs something that can say no. If your only control is a well written prompt asking it to behave, that is not a control. That is a hope.

Most of the AI-in-production conversation is still about model capability. In the environments I work in, capability stopped being the constraint a while ago. What decides whether something ships is whether anyone can prove afterwards what it did.

If you have put an agent near a production system: what actually convinced your security or compliance people? I am curious what is working elsewhere.

"Start with systems, not people"
"Reward early visibility"

I loved the talk "Postmortems Without Blame: Running Real, Transformative Incident Reviews" by Agata Skorupka, PhD at DevOpsDays London.

It linked beautifully with so much of the literature that shapes how we think about work.

Amy Edmondson's research on psychological safety ("Right Kind of Wrong") reminds us that people won't surface problems early if the culture punishes vulnerability.

L. David Marquet's "Turn the Ship Around!" shows how intent-based leadership creates conditions where responsibility is distributed, not concentrated, which makes early signals stronger.

Dan Pink's work on motivation ("Drive": autonomy, mastery, purpose) explains why engineers need more than blame or reward. They need meaning.

The emphasis on starting with systems rather than people echoes Deming's famous line: "A bad system will beat a good person every time."

It also recalls Sidney Dekker's "Just Culture", which highlights how focusing on human error blinds us to the deeper systemic issues that make failure inevitable.

And when we talk about rewarding early visibility, it's hard not to connect to Gene Kim, Jez Humble, Nicole Forsgren, and their research in Accelerate, where high-performing organisations thrive by shortening feedback loops and making work observable as soon as possible.

All of this makes me think: if we want truly transformative incident reviews, we need to design them as spaces where systems are interrogated, signals are surfaced early, and people are safe to tell the truth.

Build vs. buy is getting interesting again in the age of AI.

Last week, I had a discovery call with a credit fund that had spent the last few years trying to build its own internal system of record.

They had a CTO, an internal engineering team, and tried to build parts of what PlexAI does today around their own lending workflows.

Eventually, they decided to stop, not because they couldn’t build it.
Because building the first version turned out to be the easy part.

Maintaining it, keeping up with new models, managing token and infrastructure costs, security and compliance, integrations, edge cases, and constantly improving the product as the business evolved became a job of its own. It also meant carrying the cost of an engineering team focused on something that ultimately wasn’t their core business.

There’s another part of build vs. buy that I think gets overlooked which I think is ever more important:
The product you build internally is only as good as the knowledge you put into it. Your team may know your business extremely well, but that’s still the knowledge and experience of one firm.
A company building a product for your industry is talking to hundreds of teams like yours, seeing different workflows, edge cases, mistakes, and best practices, and putting all of that back into the product.

That feedback loop is how the product keeps getting better. You learn from every customer, not just from yourself.

It made me think about how we approach the same question at PlexAI.
We build internal tools all the time. I’m a big believer in it. If we need a small tool that automates a specific workflow for sales, operations, or customer success, we’ll build it.

But I wouldn’t build our own Notion!

There’s a big difference between building a tool and owning a system of record that your organization needs to rely on every day for years.

AI has made software much easier to build, I’m not sure it has made software any easier to own.… more

There is a lot of talk about AI safety now and the need to slow down AI development. Dario Amodei suggests independent evaluators inside the frontier labs. Many other people have similar suggestions. 

I personally think it is close to impossible to slow down technology like that. Think about like this. AI progress is not just coming from smarter frontier models. Most progress today is probably coming from organising collaborating agents. If you connect a lot of smaller models and give them each memory, notes, tools, etc, they function as an organisation. An organisation can be much smarter and more efficient than a single model. In a way, you can think of the connected agents as a distributed neural network. The agents have low bandwidth for communication unlike the layers in a standard neural network. However, that can be compensated for by scaling and parallel computing.

Compare with humans. A human society can become much "smarter" and capable by having more humans working in parallel, by linking the humans together with networks, by giving the humans better tools, and so on. 

AI progress cannot be stopped by frontier labs pausing or halting. You would need to stop production of inference chips, memory modules, links and networks, tools, orchestration, embedding of AI in industry, etc. It is equivalent to the statement that you cannot stop human progress by capping the intelligence of individuals. 

In other words, it is impossible to halt AI, and technological, progress. There is a strong message itself in that. Instead of halting or pausing development, embrace the progress and use AI to strengthen the systems. How do you build intuition for when and how AI models for developability predictions can be valuable in development of Biologics?

In this example, I use Bionamic to explore an antibody dataset from Jain et al., looking for correlations between experimental observations and predicted properties.

The screenshot below compares a predicted variable (propensity for aggregation) with an experimental measurement (HIC retention time). The result: a strong correlation (p < 1e-10). 

The aggregation propensity was predicted using Aggrescan, a structure-based tool for protein aggregation prediction. So, before running Aggrescan, the antibody structures were predicted using ABodyBuilder. This means that we're running two layers of prediction - first structure, then aggregation - yet still find a clear connection to the real Hydrophobic Interaction Chromatography measurements.

I think exercises like this are a powerful way to understand what today’s gold-standard AI tools can (and can’t!) do, and Bionamic offers a fully integrated way to run them.

AI is not just accelerating software delivery 🏎️. It is manufacturing a new attack surface across your business 💥.

More AI-generated code. 
More APIs. 
More agents. 
More MCPs. 
More workflows with real privilege and real business access.

For years, AppSec focused on code developers wrote and the software supply chain.

Now we have to secure software built by humans, models, and autonomous agents operating at machine speed. This changes the question.

It is no longer just: Are we scanning enough?
It is: Are we testing what AI is building, or just hoping the old playbook still holds?

A lot of vendors are reaching for the “AI pentesting” label right now. In many cases, they just mean LLMs crafting payloads faster. But prediction is not proof.

✅ The real question is whether you can correlate what static analysis predicts with what dynamic testing actually proves, leveraging multiple models for contextual analysis, against real running applications, at pipeline speed, continuously, and turn that into precise remediation back in the developer loop, not just another alert.

🎯That is why Snyk has been moving aggressively, from Evo as an agentic security orchestrator, to AI-native protections around tools like Claude Code and Gemini CLI, to a sharper focus on the emerging agentic supply chain around MCPs, agents, and plugins.

The leaders who stand out in this next era will not win with the best AI policy deck. They will win by answering three questions:
❓Are we testing what AI is building?
❓Can we govern what we cannot yet fully inventory?
❓Can we move fast without giving up trust and control?

That is the conversation heading into RSAC.

We just released something we’ve been wanting for a long time:

AI Schema, a Drupal module that turns your entire entity model into clean, structured JSON for LLMs.

If you’ve ever tried to explain a Drupal data model to ChatGPT or Claude… you know how painful it is.

Dozens of field types, revision tables, field storage tables, entity references everywhere…
And somehow you’re expected to explain all of this in a single prompt.

Not ideal.

So we built a shortcut.

With a single command:

drush aischema:export-all

You get a complete, LLM-friendly representation of your Drupal data model:

• Full entity & field definitions (with semantic hints)
• Relationship graph between entities
• Actual SQL table mappings
• Token-efficient compact format
• Ready-to-use SELECT queries (with correct JOINs)
• Clean, per-entity outputs

The compact format is designed specifically for LLMs:

title: str! #label
field_tags: ref[]>taxonomy_term #taxonomy
body: txt #content

This makes it much easier to:

→ Generate SQL with AI
→ Plan migrations
→ Scaffold APIs
→ Build ETL pipelines
→ Auto-generate documentation

How the #1 virtual power plant aggregator in North America builds the tools that keep the grid stable.

Voltus manages 8.5 GW of distributed energy resources: industrial HVAC, battery storage, backup generators, all coordinated to respond when the grid is under stress. Pulling that off takes market experts and engineers working on the same problems with the same tools.

Notebooks made that collaboration possible, but keeping them auditable at scale meant heavy manual process: version control by filename, hidden state that could silently break a dashboard, and interactive apps only engineers could build. Rolling out a dedicated BI platform would have taken years and created exactly the silo they were trying to avoid.

After trialing marimo in early 2025, Staff Software Engineer Will Lachance found the middle ground: a reactive engine that replaced manual verification with architectural guarantees, in pure .py files that plugged straight into the CI/CD and code review pipelines the team already used. Suddenly, analysts could ship interactive apps without touching JavaScript.

marimo apps at Voltus grew from 2 to over 35 in six months. The same notebook moves from prototype to human-verified app to scheduled automation, without rewrites. They even embedded a reactive marimo sandbox in their public API docs so partners can test dispatch integrations themselves, eliminating the usual back-and-forth of manual integration testing.

In Will's words: marimo didn't force a tradeoff. Voltus got the reproducibility and auditability a regulated, high-stakes industry demands, while their workflows became more accessible and more enjoyable to use.

How much of your balance sheet is quietly walking out the door?

Most businesses carry thousands of physical assets, everything from a laptop to the building it sits in. What happens when an AI coding workflow consumes 1.18 million tokens, modifies files across your repositories, and then returns nothing?

That happened to me today.

I was using Claude to run a multi-agent production readiness review of a WhatsApp integration. Seven agents were working through concurrency, state management, provider behaviour, testing and deployment risks.

Then the workflow hit the session limit.

The result:

"The rollout workflow failed, all seven agents hit the session limit after burning 1.18M tokens, and returned nothing. But they’d already written files before dying."

To be clear, the agents did not do nothing. Work was completed. Files were inspected and changed.

But because the workflow failed before producing its consolidated output, a new session now has to spend additional tokens investigating the repositories to determine:

• What was changed  
• Which findings were confirmed  
• Which tasks were completed  
• Whether the implementation is safe  
• What remains unfinished  

That is a serious weakness in long-running agentic software development workflows.

Progress should be checkpointed continuously, not only held inside an agent’s active context until the final response is generated.

If an agent:

• changes a file  
• confirms a root cause  
• completes a test  
• makes an architectural decision  
• identifies a production risk  

that information should be persisted in a recoverable execution record.

A session limit should interrupt the workflow, not erase its usable outcome.

The engineering work may still exist in the repositories, but reconstructing the reasoning, decisions and completion state introduces more cost, more uncertainty and more opportunities for error.

Agentic coding systems need durable state, resumable workflows and automatic synthesis checkpoints, especially when they are capable of consuming more than a million tokens in a single task.

This is not just a token usage issue. It is a reliability and product design issue.

Interested to hear how Anthropic is thinking about recoverability for long running Claude Code and multiagent workflows.

Six banks, NatWest and ING among them, published a set of principles for 𝐚𝐠𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐢𝐜 𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐦𝐞𝐫𝐜𝐞 on Tuesday. 

Transparency. 
Safety. 
Privacy and data. 
Choice. 
Interoperability.

The first principle asks two things. That everyone in a transaction knows an agent is involved and on whose behalf it acts. And that a record is kept of what was instructed, authenticated and done.

My reading is that this expectation is not new. Article 50 of the #EUAIAct has required since August that people are told when they are dealing with an AI system.
So the questions are not new either. Which agent this is. Who owns it. What it is allowed to do. What evidence exists of what it did.

Every bank has to answer these today. An agent without those four answers is not ready to act as a counterparty.

The encouraging part is that none of this asks us to invent a discipline. We have kept registers of owners, approved scopes and evidence for models for years, and that methodology carries over to agents largely intact.

What has to change is where the registration happens. A model could be entered by hand, because there were few and each took months to build. An agent takes an afternoon and anyone can build one, so the entry has to be created at build time by the platform itself, as a by-product of deployment rather than a form somebody remembers to complete.
Do that, and the answer to the merchant's question is already sitting there when it is asked.

To address that scale, three themes kept coming back:
1. Treat risk management as an engineering challenge, not just a governance process.
2. Structure the inventory so that the components of an agent, its skills, guardrails, and tools, are governed separately rather than as one black box.
3. Separate governance into a runtime part and an offline part.

“Alice: i giorni della droga” viene pubblicato nel 1971 come il diario, anonimo, di un’ adolescente precipitata nella dipendenza. 
Il libro si presenta come una testimonianza intima e brutale su come possa nascere una tossicofilia.
Alice ha solo 15 anni. 
L’età delle cotte deludenti, del bisogno di appartenere, della necessità di trovare il proprio posto nel mondo. 
L’ umore e la progettualità futura variano in base a come tali elementi si muovono.
Alice ha solo 15 anni ma già sperimenta il vuoto esistenziale; festeggia il proprio compleanno e nella pagina di diario dedicata a questa ricorrenza, scrive solo una riga che si conclude con la parola “niente”. 
Il primo incontro con la droga è puramente ludico, anzi quasi la spaventa. Da subito però ne è fatalmente attratta: un sollievo immediato da quel vuoto che la torment. Crede di avere controllo sull’uso, come se fosse un interruttore da accendere e spegnere a proprio piacimento. Ma il punto tragico del romanzo è proprio questo: l’illusione del controllo precede spesso la perdita dello stesso. La tossicofilia diventa il modo con cui gestisce gli stressors quotidiani. Nel suo percorso compare anche il ricovero psichiatrico: una terra di nessuno, ove convive la possibilità di cura ma anche vissuti di alienazione. Alice prova a immaginare un futuro diverso, le ultime pagine sono pagine di speranza, Alice sembra esserne uscita.
La protagonista muore circa 3 settimane dopo aver scritto l’ultima pagina. I suoi genitori la trovano morta.
Overdose? Suicidio? Incidente? Il libro lascia il mistero aperto.
Non scevro da controversie riguardo la sua autenticità, il piccolo volume non offre una morale rassicurante, uno spaccato su quel vuoto che Alice ha tentato di colmare a carissimo prezzo.

Our Story
MedBook Global is an early-stage HealthTech startup building an AI-powered platform that simplifies dental medical tourism by helping patients find trusted clinics, compare treatment options, and make informed healthcare decisions.
Every great company begins with a problem worth solving. Ours began with a personal journey.
For more than two decades, I experienced healthcare not as a founder, but as a patient. That journey taught me something no textbook, conference, or business plan ever could: when people face important medical decisions, they need more than access to clinics. They need clarity, transparency, trusted guidance, and confidence that they are making the right choice.
Over the years, I met outstanding healthcare professionals, explored medical systems across different countries, and saw firsthand how difficult it can be for patients to navigate treatment abroad. Information is often fragmented, pricing lacks transparency, and building trust across borders remains one of the biggest challenges in medical tourism.
Rather than accepting these challenges as inevitable, I saw an opportunity to build something better—not only for myself, but for millions of patients facing the same uncertainty.
That vision became MedBook Global.
Together with a team of engineer, and AI specialist, we are building a platform that combines artificial intelligence with human expertise to simplify every step of the patient journey—from the first consultation to selecting the right clinic and planning treatment abroad.
We believe technology should remove complexity, not create it.
Our mission is to make medical travel transparent, trustworthy, and accessible by giving every patient the information and confidence they need to make informed healthcare decisions.
As an Estonia-based early-stage HealthTech startup, we are committed to building long-term partnerships with verified clinics while creating a trusted digital ecosystem for international patients.
Because the future of medical tourism is not simply about connecting patients with clinics.
It's about building trust before the journey even begins.

💁‍♀️ The Ukrainian digital envoys of the e-Governance Academy (eGA) had a friendly meeting with US Ambassador to Estonia, George P. Kent.

At the meeting, the envoys presented their projects supporting the Ukrainian community in Estonia under the US Department of State-financed project “Digital Empowerment of the Ukrainian Community in Estonia” (DEUCE).

💻 In addition to facilitating the use of everyday Estonian and Ukrainian e-services, the digital envoys from Ukraine also played a crucial role in familiarizing local Ukrainians with digital tools and solutions.

During the meeting, Ambassador Kent was introduced to the initiatives undertaken by the digital envoys:
📍 Tartu Help Bot: A Telegram bot providing essential information to Ukrainian refugees regarding refugee status and integration resources.
📍 Scam Map: A visual guide highlighting common fraud schemes and preventive measures to safeguard the Ukrainian community in Estonia from financial and psychological harm.
📍 Professional Development Workshop: Workshops aimed at equipping Ukrainians with essential digital skills for success in the Estonian job market.
📍 Easy Stuudium: A project facilitating the use of essential educational programs for Ukrainian children and their parents in Estonia.

"For eGA, which primarily operates outside Estonia, this is our unique opportunity to collaborate within Estonia for the benefit of the Ukrainian people," said Kristina Mänd, lead of the project.

💡 In the first cohort, eGA engaged 31 talented young Ukrainians living in Estonia, training them as digital envoys, who have since reached over 10,000 Ukrainians, educating and empowering over 400 digitally vulnerable community members.

The project DEUCE, or “Digital Empowerment of the Ukrainian Community in Estonia”, is slated to continue until September 2025 and is being implemented by eGA with support from the United States Department of State, totaling $236,000.

Allocation. Coordination. Evaluation. Correction. And setting the objective.

Agreement is not verification.

The danger was never rebellion. It is correlated error. Failure that arrives everywhere at once, because everything was built from the same assumptions.
Which is why the question to ask of any autonomous process is not how many layers of review sit above it.

It is simpler. Where does this touch the world, and how quickly do we find out when it was wrong.

AI agents just became cheaper than offshore labour.

After several years of promised ROI from AI, the economics are starting to work.

A new analysis from a16z estimates that a computer-using AI agent now costs $6–8 per hour, compared with roughly $10 per hour for an offshore worker.

But what matters beyond cost are the practicalities. Rather than wrestling with staff turnover, time-zone differences and variable output, firms can invest in agents that:
 1. Work 24/7.
 2. Respond to feedback immediately – and remember it.
 3. Scale as the workload increases.

This won’t eliminate offshore labour, but it will change the nature of the work and expectations of output – just as it will for onshore teams.

That means less time spent on repetitive processes and more time supervising agents, reviewing exceptions and improving workflows.

For accounting firms, the limiting factor will increasingly be neither headcount nor labour cost. It will be how quickly they can turn their internal knowledge into clear, controlled and auditable processes for agents to follow.

Firms have spent years learning how to scale people across their systems. The next challenge is making those systems ready for agents – not just one agent completing one task, but hundreds working in parallel with the right access, controls and oversight.

If you're in a growth phase right now — hiring steadily, crossing state lines, adding benefits complexity — this is the right time to look at your payroll and HR infrastructure. Not when you've hit 200 employees and the problems are impossible to ignore.

Wellness plans in pet insurance are often treated like add-ons. The data suggests they may be something much more important: an engagement layer that actively changes the shape of risk.

In Odie Pet Insurance's data, we found that dogs without a wellness plan are:
1.85× more likely to file a $1k+ claim
2.3× more likely to file a $2.5k+ claim
2.7× more likely to file a $5k+ claim

That’s not just a claims pattern. It’s a product insight.

Dogs with an active wellness plan show what I think of as the “monitored pet” pattern: more routine touchpoints, earlier detection, and fewer catastrophic spikes.

Dogs without a wellness plan show the opposite: fewer visits, but bigger bills when they do appear.

So what’s the takeaway?

Wellness is an opportunity for pet insurers to reframe the relationship between insurer and insured.

When pet parents engage with a wellness plan, they are no longer passive policyholders waiting for reimbursement after something goes wrong. They become active partners in managing their pet’s health risk.

That matters because insurers are not just paying claims. We are also trying to manage the risk profile of the population we insure.

Wellness gives us a mechanism to do that by aligning incentives with the pet parent: more routine care, earlier intervention, better visibility, and fewer catastrophic outcomes.

In other words, wellness turns engagement into risk management.… more

Excited to finally share what we've been working on with one of our earliest customers, who has now deployed millions of stateful agents in production - Bilt.

Today, companies store data about their customers in legacy databases and CRMs like Salesforce. In the near future, the native format for customer data will be living AI memories. Bilt is one of those rare companies sitting at the bleeding edge of applied AI and is a sneak peak into the future of how businesses understand their customers.

Before Letta, Bilt used traditional black-box recommender systems to turn customer data into rankings to place offers inside their app. But in the age of AI agents, the team at Bilt wanted to do more: what if you could have an AI system that could actually learn about users from their transactions, and dynamically adjust its understanding of the user over time?

In their early experiments with the latest Anthropic and OpenAI models, Bilt immediately ran into context window limitations. What Bilt really needed was a system where an AI agent could have an infinite context window and store a compressed "memory" of the user's preferences over weeks, months, and even years. This was exactly what we had developed with our latest research on Sleep-time Compute.

How does it work?

Each user on the Bilt platform gets their own swarm of stateful agents that live in the cloud. There's dozens of agents per-user that keep track of a "category-specific memories". The multi-agent system makes heavy use of key concepts that are unique to Letta such as self-editing memory blocks and multi-agent shared memory.

The end result?

The most advanced agent deployment in the world (outside of the handful of frontier AI labs). Bilt isn't just running workflows or "agents" that call OpenAI inside a Python script - they are running a deployment of over a million stateful agents that have self-editing memory, consuming billions of tokens while learning from a constant firehose of customer data.

Bilt is literally living in the future where every company has a living & breathing copy of every customer sitting inside of a stateful agent. And the secret to making it all work is memory.

It's been an absolute pleasure working with the Bilt team on this project, special shout-out to Andrew Fitz, Kosta Krauth, Ankur Jain, and Will Laughlin

Today we're launching Agent File (.af) 👾 – solving one of the biggest challenges in AI development by making stateful agents truly portable and shareable for the first time.

This open standard file format encapsulates everything that makes an LLM-driven agent intelligent: core memory blocks, tool configurations, memory management settings, and model parameters – all in a single file that can be easily shared and deployed across environments.

Agent File was built to address key challenges in the agent ecosystem:
* 🔄 Portability: Move agents between systems or deploy them to new environments
* 🤝 Collaboration: Share your agents with other developers and the community
* 💾 Preservation: Archive agent configurations to preserve your work
* 📝 Versioning: Track changes to agents over time through a standardized format

The Agent File format supports a variety of agent types, including:
* Research agents with search, planning, and memory capabilities
* Customer support agents with specialized tools for external APIs
* Workflow automation agents for LLM-driven deterministic processes
* MemGPT-based agents with advanced memory management

Introducing the AI agents stack: breaking down today’s tech stack for building AI agents into three key layers: (1) agent hosting/serving, (2) agent frameworks, (3) LLM models & storage.

Sarah Wooders and I got so tired of seeing bad “market maps” for LLM / AI agents shoved in our feeds that either had layouts that made no sense or were littered with random companies on them (ie that don’t have serious community adoption), or both. As researchers / engineers actually working in the agents space, we decided to make a serious attempt at making one of these market map diagrams that actually reflects real world usage by today’s developers building AI agents.

Basically - if you’re starting a vertical agents company today (November 2024), what software are you most likely to use to build out your “agents stack”?

In our opinion, the AI/LLM agents stack is a significant departure from the standard LLM stack. The key difference between the two lies in managing state: LLM serving platforms are generally stateless, whereas agent serving platforms need to be stateful (retain the state of the agent server-side).

Building stateful services is a lot harder of an engineering challenge compared to building developer SDKs, so unsurprisingly very few agent serving platforms actually exist today (Letta being one of them).

For a full breakdown of the stack, check out our full post (link in comments).

Today we're releasing the Letta Agent SDK - an SDK for building and deploying stateful agents running on frontier coding harnesses. It's fully open source and supports local, self-hosted, and managed cloud deployments.

This is the first SDK that allows you to build the same stateful agent once, and access it from anywhere - teleporting it between devices, without losing any of its learned context and memories.

Why didn't this exist before? The last generation of agent frameworks were relatively simple - they executed tools in a loop, and "deploying" an agent often meant just deploying the code. More advanced stateful APIs existed that separated the concept of session state and client (OpenAI Responses API and the Letta V1 API), but the client was still quite simple.

This is what the Agent SDK is built for - programatic control of stateful agents with a harness you can deploy anywhere: locally, self-hosted, or fully managed in the cloud. MemFS is baked in, so you get git-tracked memory with zero setup.

Today we're releasing "trajectory", an open source package for normalizing traces from coding agents into a standard format, with day-1 support for Claude Code, Codex, Pi, OpenClaw, Letta Code, Hermes Agent, LangChain DeepAgents - with more agent harnesses on the way.

Trajectory lets you turn all your local agent data (e.g. your Claude Code and Codex transcripts) into a standardized JSON format that's ~5x+ more token efficient than the native jsonl format.

Why is this important? Two words: continual learning.

The data you generate while using coding agents is a treasure trove of data that can be mined to create durable memories that help prevent your agent from repeating the same mistakes in the future. This is what we call "agent dreaming" - turning experience data into memories.

👾 Today we're launching Letta Code, a memory-first coding agent that actually learns about you, your team, and your codebase over time. It's completely open source, and is world's best performing model-agnostic OSS coding harness.

How is Letta Code different from Claude Code? Firstly, it's open source and model-agnostic. Claude Code is closed source and locked down to Anthropic's Claude models.

Perhaps more importantly, Letta Code is *memory-first*. What does this mean?

In Claude Code (and every other coding CLI), every time you want to work on a task, you type `claude` (or `codex`, etc), and spin up a new "agent". The agent is brand new - it doesn't know anything about you, and has real history of prior interactions (for example, it can't "look back" on previous messages to figure out what you were working on last week).

In contrast, Letta Code is fully stateful. The idea is that you work with a small handful of agents that get better and better over time as they learn more about you and your codebase. Think of it like working with humans: every time a Letta Code agent makes a mistake, you teach it what it did wrong so that it can remember to never make the same mistake.

In Letta Code, can use the `/init` command to have your agent do "deep research" on your codebase, and the `/remember` command to guide it when it makes mistakes. Your investment in teaching your agent is rewarded. I've personally been using the same Letta Code agent to build Letta Code itself for the past ~3 weeks straight, and its learning more every day.

Letta Code isn't just for coding - it's a general purpose CLI harness that you can use to connect *any* Letta agent to your computer. For example, if you have a personal assistant agent running on a remote Letta server, you can use the Letta Code CLI to "beam" that agent down into your terminal to give it access to your computer (and all your files / programs).

The central thesis of our research at Letta is continual learning in token space.

If you're in AI you've probably seen the term "continual learning" flooding your feed, especially post-NeurIPS. At a high level, the intuition behind this exitement is clear: LLMs in 2025 are incredibly intelligent and capable agents, but the limiting factor has clearly become memory (or "learning") - even the best agents like ChatGPT or Claude Code don't meaningfully learn over time (the model weights are frozen), which caps their utility.

So what's the solution? "Continual learning" is a long-standing area of research (since the 1980s!) that focuses on how to update neural network weights over time as new data arrives. It turns out that continually updating the weights of a neural network is an incredibly difficult problem: the same techniques used by the big model labs for pre/mid/post-training don't transfer to the continual learning setting.

But this narrow focus continual learning through weight updates is misguided. The modern LLM agent is not just defined by its model weights, but also by its context (system prompts, tool definitions, conversation history), and different contexts with the same underlying model can produce dramatically different "agents".

Instead, more researchers should focus on continual learning not through weight updates, but instead through learning in *token space*. Recent research hypothesizes that the transformer actually learns to approximate gradient descent *within* its forward pass of inference, which explains the incredibly powerful property of LLMs to learn and adapt through in-context token updates.

Reframing continual learning as "learning contexts" instead of "learning weights" also clarifies how existing work on prompt optimization such as DSPy and GEPA fit into the continual learning narrative: these approaches solve a local version of the "token-space continual learning" problem, DSPy through Bayesian optimization, and GEPA through natural language reflection.

In contrast, the full continual learning problem requires learning contexts across an open-ended sequence of tasks that spans months or even years, where a single "agent" will have a lifespan that far exceeds that of any underlying model. Imagine the same agent with the same memories, but across GPT-5 in 2025 to GPT-15 in 2030.

This is the setting that we hyperfocused on at Letta, starting with our original work on MemGPT. The continual learning problem is still far from solved, and will require further advances in offline memory refinement (sleep-time compute) and model training to teach agents to manage their own contexts. We also believe that token-space learning and weight-space learning should be combined, and predict a future where memories in token space are progressively distilled into model weights for personalization and efficiency gains.

Ministrei uma sessão focada em Apache Kafka, abordando desde a base conceitual até a engenharia de alta resiliência que sustenta o ecossistema do iFood, conectando a teoria através de analogias do dia a dia à prática real de grandes volumes de dados.
Durante a mentoria, mergulhamos fundo em tópicos essenciais para arquiteturas orientadas a eventos:

Fundamentos Sólidos: Mensagens, tópicos, brokers, clusters, partições, offsets e as dinâmicas de Consumer Groups para processamento paralelo e independente.

Garantia de Ordenação e Resiliência: Como mitigar problemas como Hot Partitions usando chaves inteligentes e como o Schema Registry (com foco em regras de compatibilidade como Backward) funciona como um verdadeiro contrato de API seguro.

Arquitetura e Decisões Técnicas: Comparações práticas entre Kafka vs. SQS/SNS para múltiplos consumidores e como arquitetamos casos de uso críticos (como User Profile).

Abstrações e Observabilidade: Como bibliotecas internas no iFood mitigam a complexidade de baixo nível para os desenvolvedores e a importância de middlewares para controle de taxa (Rate Limit), Retries, Dead Letter Queues (DLQ) e observabilidade via Datadog. 

Mais do que apenas passar conteúdo, foi incrível ver a troca de experiências, as dúvidas excelentes trazidas pela turma e o engajamento na parte prática da implementação.
Fica aqui o meu agradecimento imenso ao comitê do < Go! para Elas /> e a todo o time do iFood pelo convite e pela confiança em me deixar liderar esse momento. Ver iniciativas como o Elas São Tech impulsionando o talento feminino na tecnologia me dá ainda mais orgulho do caminho que venho construindo como desenvolvedora.

Parabéns a todas as participantes pelo nível técnico e pelas discussões! O futuro da tecnologia é de vocês. 💜

View company: Quantumeon.ai
Quantumeon.ai

5mo

Why most "synthetic data" is statistical mimicry — and what validation actually requires.

A five-level framework:

1. Statistical fidelity — distributions match. Necessary but insufficient.

2. Structural validity — relational patterns preserved. Network topology, correlation structure.

3. Behavioral plausibility — would a domain expert recognize these as real agents?

4. Mechanistic grounding — is there a causal theory explaining WHY the data looks this way?

5. Reconstructive validation — can the model reproduce known historical outcomes?

Most vendors stop at Level 1. We published the full framework — including the failure modes at each level — because we think validation should be publishable, not proprietary.

Really pleased to say we supported a great human into a new role this week, as a Head of IT.

I want to talk about the 11 months before that though.

He was exceptional through the process, and his references backed that up without hesitation. One of the strongest candidate profiles we've put in front of a customer this year.

He'd also been out of work for 11 months, applying for roles he was clearly qualified for and, in the main, hearing nothing back.

He was being selective, and rightly so. But that doesn't explain the silence, because plenty of what he went for was squarely in his lane.

A gap on a CV gets read as a verdict. If he's been available that long, somebody else must have seen something. So it goes on the maybe pile, and the maybe pile never gets read.

That's unconscious bias in practice.

Nobody decides to do it. It happens in the few seconds a CV gets before it's onto the next, which is why nobody ever catches themselves at it.

So if you're hiring and you've got a strong CV with a gap on it, ask about the gap instead of assuming you already know what it means. The answer is usually a restructure, a company that ran out of runway, or someone who decided not to take the first thing that came along.

Get that wrong and you'll miss the best match in the pile without ever knowing it was there.… more

Over the past few months, I’ve been working on an idea around Active Directory security and attack paths.

We already have great tools that help us understand AD relationships and identify potential attack paths.

But I wanted to explore another question:
What happens after we discover those paths?
Can we connect them with what our SOC is actually seeing?

Can we map the activity to MITRE ATT&CK? Or simulate the attack using RedCanary ?

Can we identify when an attack path may actually be getting exercised?

And, in a controlled and authorized environment, can we validate whether our security controls can detect it?

That led to BlindSpot.
The current version includes:

• Active Directory security assessment
• Attack-path discovery
• Privilege and ACL analysis
• SIEM log correlation
• MITRE ATT&CK mapping
• Detection visibility around discovered paths
• Controlled attack-path validation workflows
• Security findings and remediation guidance

The concept is simple:
Discover the path → Monitor the activity → Map it to ATT&CK → Validate detection → Remediate → Test again.

I’m now opening the BlindSpot Community Version for FREE.

I don’t want this to be something I build in isolation.

I want people from the AD, SOC, Blue Team, Red Team, Purple Team and security research communities to test it and tell me where it works — and more importantly, where it doesn’t.

Find bugs.
Challenge the findings.
Find false positives.
Find false negatives.
Suggest improvements.

It’s a community version, so community feedback is part of the product.

Sometimes you need to give something back. ❤️

How to Scale Infrastructure from Thousands to Millions of Users
Scaling isn’t just about adding more servers—it’s about making every resource work efficiently while keeping performance, security, and costs under control.
If you're struggling with slow response times, outages, or high costs, here’s how to scale properly. 👇

1️⃣ Fix Bottlenecks Before Scaling
Scaling without optimizing is like upgrading a car with a broken engine.
✅ Database optimization – Indexing, query tuning, caching
✅ Efficient load balancing – Traffic should be evenly distributed
✅ Automate deployments – Remove manual inefficiencies
🔹 Rule #1: Optimize before scaling.

2️⃣ Build a Cloud Architecture That Scales
✅ Kubernetes for container orchestration
✅ Microservices over monolithic applications
✅ GitOps-driven CI/CD Pipelines
✅ Cloud cost optimization – Right-sizing, auto-scaling, and spot instances
🚀 Results: Faster deployments, reduced infrastructure costs, and high availability.

3️⃣ Optimize Configurations for Performance & Cost
Scaling doesn’t just mean adding resources—it means using existing ones smarter.
✅ Fine-tune Kubernetes CPU & memory limits
✅ Optimize database indexing & queries
✅ Tweak app configurations (JVM, PHP, etc.)
✅ Implement automated scaling rules
🎯 Impact: Lower costs, fewer resource bottlenecks, and stable performance under heavy loads.

4️⃣ Improve Performance with Caching & Load Balancing
Don’t overload the database—use caching & load balancing!
✅ Redis/Memcached – Reduces DB hits
✅ NGINX/HAProxy for smart traffic distribution
✅ API rate limiting – Prevents abuse & overload
⚡ Result: Dramatically improved API response time & system efficiency.

5️⃣ Observability & Monitoring 🔍
Scaling without monitoring is like driving blindfolded.
✅ Prometheus & Grafana – Monitor system health in real time
✅ ELK Stack – Debug issues faster
✅ Service Mesh (Istio, Linkerd) – Traffic control & security
🔹 Outcome: Fewer outages, faster root-cause analysis.

6️⃣ Security & Compliance at Scale 🛡️
Security must scale with your infrastructure:
✅ IAM & least privilege access
✅ CI/CD security scanning
✅ Enhanced compliance through automation (PCI DSS, ISO27001)
✅ Encrypted communication (TLS, VPNs)
🔹 Outcome: Reduced major security incidents and improved security posture.

🚀 Final Takeaways
✔ Fix bottlenecks before adding resources
✔ Optimizing configurations is just as important as scaling
✔ Automation is key—Manual processes kill growth
✔ Monitoring & security should never be an afterthought
