Never build three big features in a row

Stack three big features back to back, no let-up between them, and the work will grind you flat. You will find exhausted and mentally drained. None of them has to be hard. You just never get to put the load down. I have done it to myself more than once, and I have learned to never ask the same to my team!

When you build something new you carry the whole thing in your head: the data model, the edge cases, the place it all falls over if you get the order wrong. Hold that for a week, then start the next one and hold all of that too, then the one after, and the weight just keeps stacking. Nothing comes off the pile.
There is a limit to how much of it you can do well. 

Bug fixing asks almost nothing of you by comparison. A wrong label, a query sorting the wrong way, the twenty-minute fix that ships. You open it, you close it, you watch the test go green. (Some bugs are brutal and eat a whole day, sure. Those are features wearing a bug's clothes. I mean the small ones.) However, doing only bug fixing will make you feel undervalued.

The best option is to break the pattern every once in a while. I don't mean working a few hours on a feature, then jumping on a bugfix, and then back to the feature. The context switch will eat you alive. No, I mean do your feature, maybe two if they are not massive, then use a short sprint to fix a list of issues. A cooldown sprint.

Cooldown sprints are critical, not just because every feature will undoubtedly carry minor fixes, but because you need to ensure your development team won't burn out.

If the only thing you focus on is to push new features out, without a care in the world for the wellbeing of your team, you will have high turnover, and unhappy developers. And these two things are the perfect storm you would steering your project towards.… more

🇬🇧 English version

There's a question that comes up, sooner or later, in every status review: "so where do we actually stand?"
The Gantt chart is right there, dense with colored bars, symbols, percentages. And yet that question keeps coming back, because a Gantt chart tells you what was planned, not how the project is really going in one synthetic view; this ends up forcing endless extra slides and long words and descriptions just to explain, in the end, where things actually stand. Too often, on top of that, the impact of the risks weighing on the project isn't properly accounted for, or represented in the project plan.

Over the years I've explained and helped implement, across very different projects, a method that let me answer exactly that question: the S-Curve. A simple model, buildable with nothing more than an Excel sheet, that turns activities, effort, and risk into a single objective curve, able to show a project's real status at a glance, in one single synthetic number. 

I've watched it work so many times, with teams and executives alike, that I decided it deserved a book: not just the "how," but also the "why it works," the logic and reasoning that shaped it over time.

"The Magic S-Curve," the second title in the TechEssentials series, is now available in both Italian and English, in paperback and Kindle, on Amazon KDP (https://a.co/d/033PH2mw)

What the book is about

In three parts, the book explains why the Gantt chart alone isn't enough, how to build the S-Curve step by step, and how to read it at every level, from the executive summary for the sponsor down to the operational detail for the team. An optional appendix also shows how to automate the entire process with the help of an AI assistant.

As the title suggests, after the first presentations by a team adopting this method, a little magic always happens: the status review slides shrink, the meeting starts opening with the same single question every time, "so where do we stand with the Curve?", and finally everyone, from the team to the sponsor, looks at the same number and understands the same thing.

If you work with IT projects, cybersecurity, ICT risk management, or managing complexity, I hope it catches your interest and maybe proves useful. And if you do read it, I'd genuinely like to hear your take: criticism and suggestions are always welcome, hoped for even.

Elixir 🤝 Rust: Task.async(fn -> Rust.performant() end)

What actually happens when BEAM resilience meets Rust performance?

Florian Gilcher and Leandro Pereira join BEAM There, Done That to talk NIFs, ports, hybrid architectures, and why “just rewrite it in Rust” isn’t always the answer

https://lnkd.in/e36rZ3Ey

Modern backend systems are increasingly shaped by two competing forces: reliability at scale and the demand for performance. Few ecosystems embody these forces as clearly as the BEAM and Rust. One prioritizes fault tolerance, distribution, and soft real-time guarantees; the other delivers precise control over memory and CPU with zero-cost abstractions. The question is no longer which one to choose, but how to combine them effectively.

Systems built on the BEAM through languages like are designed around failure. Lightweight processes, supervision trees, and message passing make it possible to build applications that recover automatically and degrade gracefully under pressure. This model works well for distributed systems, high-availability applications, and real-time communication. The trade-off is that the BEAM is not optimized for heavy computation and low-level memory control.

Rust provides predictable performance and memory safety without garbage collection, making it ideal for CPU-intensive workloads, data processing, systems integration, and latency-sensitive operations. Rust removes many common memory and concurrency bugs while maintaining high performance, making it a strong complement to Elixir.

Integration can happen through Native Implemented Functions (NIFs), which allow Elixir to call Rust directly with minimal overhead, or through external processes, which provide stronger isolation at the cost of communication overhead. Modern tooling has also made safer Rust integrations easier.
A practical strategy is to treat Elixir as the orchestration layer and Rust as the execution engine for specialized tasks. Elixir manages workflows, supervision, and distribution while Rust handles performance-critical computation.

This hybrid approach introduces challenges, including increased complexity, harder debugging across languages and deployment overhead. For that reason, Rust should not be introduced prematurely. The BEAM can handle far more than many developers assume, and optimization should be driven by bottlenecks rather than speculation.

The combination of Elixir and Rust represents a compelling model for modern systems design. One provides resilience and scalability; the other offers precision and performance. Used together, they enable a pragmatic approach: build most of the system in a fault-tolerant environment, then selectively drop to native code when performance demands it.

E que está ganhando espaço na comunidade, inicialmente usada como engine de Markdown para o BeaconCMS e atualmente usada em projetos da comunidade incluindo Ash AI, Tableau, Algora, Exmeralda, entre outros.

Nessa talk iremos conhecer na prática alguns desses recursos como o parser em Rust implementado com NIF, manipulação de AST usando protocolos Enumerable e Collectable, o sigil ~MD que converte Markdown para formatos HTML, XML, JSON, e Delta em tempo de compilação, syntax highlighting com Tree-sitter e temas Neovim, emojis, plugins com pipeline, e mais.

Over the past few years, the way I think about technology has changed quite a bit.

Working on different projects, making difficult decisions and solving real problems has taught me that technology itself is rarely the hardest part. The real challenge is often discovering the problem that actually needs to be solved.

It is not enough to listen to a request and turn it into a list of requirements. You need to understand the context, see the problem from the other person's perspective and ask the right questions. What someone asks for is not always what they actually need, and understanding that difference takes time, curiosity and, above all, the ability to listen.

Good decisions also depend on much more than what is technically possible. Timing matters. Priorities matter. The people who will have to live with those decisions matter too.

Part of the job is being able to anticipate problems and understand the consequences of the choices we make, without falling into the trap of trying to solve today every problem that might exist tomorrow.

I've also learned that the best decisions are rarely made in isolation.

Building good products and good teams requires trust, context and room to question things. It means understanding what motivates people, listening to different perspectives and creating an environment where someone can say "I disagree" or "there's a problem here" and know they will be heard.

It also means being comfortable saying "I don't know", asking more questions and changing your mind when new information or better arguments come along.

The longer I work in technology, the more I realise that a large part of the job is not really about technology at all.

It is about understanding problems, people and context. It is about making responsible decisions and taking responsibility for what follows, not just until something is delivered, but afterwards too.

That is probably one of the most important lessons I'm taking with me into the next chapter of my professional life.

Technology matters. But the best solutions start long before the technology does.

This feels like the right moment to take those lessons and build something around the way I believe technology should be understood, designed and delivered.

There are a few things that have become very clear to me after years of working with and leading people.

One of them is simple: people have a life beyond work, and sometimes that life has to come first.

Sometimes someone joins a company and, just a few weeks later, loses their mother. In that moment, the most important question is not how many days a policy allows. It is simply: take the time you need. Come back when you are ready.

Other times, someone goes above and beyond during a particularly demanding period. It might be an urgent delivery, a certification, or a problem that simply had to be solved. A thank-you can be a message. But it can also mean taking a little time to find out what that person likes and sending them a small gesture, even from thousands of kilometres away.

And sometimes someone is going through something genuinely difficult and there is nothing we can really fix. We can still show that we noticed. It might be a huge teddy bear for a child going through a hard time. It might be an experience for two people some time later. It could be anything.

The gift itself is not the point. The gesture is. It is about someone feeling remembered as a person, not just as someone they work with.

I have always thought this was fairly basic.

People give companies a significant part of their lives. They solve problems outside working hours, answer calls they probably had no obligation to answer, take responsibility, care about customers, help colleagues, carry difficult projects and, quite often, take the company’s problems home with them.

That is why I sometimes struggle with the way we talk about culture, trust, commitment or teamwork as if they were things we could define in a presentation, a list of values or a page on a website.

To me, culture shows itself much more clearly when there is nothing to gain from the gesture.

When someone is having a difficult time.

When someone has done more than was expected.

When it would be much easier to simply follow the process.

And also when the time comes to make a difficult decision.

A professional relationship can end. For financial reasons, because of strategy, because of disagreements, or simply because it is time to go in different directions. That is part of working life.

What should not happen is for respect, consideration and everything that came before to disappear the moment that relationship is no longer convenient for the company.

If, for years, we expect people to treat the company’s problems as if they were their own, then we should also be able to remember that there is a person on the other side when it is our turn to make a difficult decision.

We will not always be able to control the decisions we have to make as leaders.

But we can control how we treat people when we make them.

And, to me, that is when a company’s culture really shows.… more

The more experience I gain, the clearer it becomes that the hardest problems are rarely technological.

Technology gives us tools, patterns, and countless ways to build a solution. The difficulty often comes before that: truly understanding the problem, the context around it, and the constraints that never make it into a technical specification. Then comes choosing, among several possible options, the one that makes the most sense at that particular moment.

In practice, there is rarely a perfect decision. You have to balance speed, quality, security, cost, complexity, and operational reality. There are times to simplify, and others when simplifying too much simply means postponing a problem that someone else will have to solve later.

I’ve also learned to place less and less value on a good decision if it doesn’t survive execution. An architecture can make perfect sense on paper and still fail when it meets existing systems, deadlines, people, dependencies, customers, or simply the reality of operating what has been built.

About the job
About Courtyard

Courtyard.io is the fastest-growing collectibles startup, ever. We are revolutionizing the world of collectibles trading by enabling instant liquidity and delivering a high-velocity, immersive experience. From trading cards to comics, we're redefining how people discover, collect, and unlock value.

Courtyard is not just another marketplace. All assets are securely vaulted and fully insured, giving collectors peace of mind alongside unmatched speed and simplicity. Whether you're investing, discovering, or curating your dream collection, we've built a platform that's trusted, simple, and built for speed.

And we're just getting started. We're a remote-first company hiring across all functions to push the boundaries of what's possible in collectibles and digital ownership.

Job Summary

Courtyard is hiring a Staff Data Engineer to own the data foundation our pricing and ML run on, from raw external market data all the way to models making decisions in production. We price and buy back assets in real time off a fragmented external market. Turning that into something a model can safely consume, and keeping the model healthy once it's live, is the hardest data problem here. You'll be the senior-most data engineering voice in a lean data org and the person who gets data science work from notebook to production. You'll own architecture and standards rather than a ticket queue.

What You'll Do

Own external market data ingestion end to end — acquisition, normalization, and delivery into the warehouse
Own the canonical item model and the entity resolution that maps messy inbound records onto it
Build quality and monitoring that catches gaps and degradation before a stakeholder notices
Own the warehouse layer (dbt modeling, tests, documentation) and set schema contracts with product engineering so upstream changes break the build, not the metrics
Build the feature and training data layer: point-in-time correct, reproducible, and consistent between training and serving
Partner with data scientists to take models from prototype to production — batch and real-time scoring, versioning, CI/CD, and safe rollout and rollback
Own model observability — input drift, prediction quality, and retraining triggers — so a degrading model gets caught by an alert, not by a bad decision
Productionize LLM-assisted pipelines where they earn their keep, with evaluation and cost controls built in
Set the engineering bar for the data org and level up DS on production-path work

What We're Looking For

7+ years across data engineering, ML engineering, or ML platform work with real production ownership, at senior or staff scope
Experience taming third-party data at volume — unstable sources, schema drift, no advance notice
Entity resolution in practice, including the judgment to know when a confident match is wrong
You've shipped ML to production alongside data scientists: built the feature pipelines, deployment path, and monitoring for models that served live decisions, not just handed off a table
Fluency in where ML breaks in the data: leakage, point-in-time joins, train/serve skew, drift
Deep SQL and Python; production dbt with tests and incremental models you actually maintained
Strong dimensional modeling — SCD Type 2, incremental loads, backfills, late-arriving data
Cloud warehouse depth. We run BigQuery and GCP; 
Comfortable with orchestration, containers, and CI/CD — you can get a service deployed and keep it observable without being an infrastructure specialist
Clear communicator with strong ownership instincts — you say what you'll own, what you won't, and by when
Bonus: feature store or model registry experience; LLM evaluation and cost management; pricing or valuation systems; a real interest in trading cards and collectibles

Most agent code can run as batch. Almost nobody runs it that way.

Your agent is a system prompt, a tool set, and a loop: call the model, execute tools in-process, repeat. On-demand is priced for someone waiting on the answer. Run 50,000 records overnight and nobody is waiting. You are paying a rush fee on work that is not in a rush.

With OpenRelay, the fix is one flag: batch=True.

Works on:
- Vercel AI SDK
- OpenAI Agents SDK
- LangGraph
- Pydantic AI

Same agent definition, same system prompt, same tools, same schemas.

Under the hood:

1. Your tools live behind an MCP server or a plain HTTP API instead of running inside application code.
2. The inference runs as a batch job, at batch rates.
3. When the model emits a tool call, the batch runtime reaches out to your server, feeds the result back, and continues the loop.

No rewrite, no new framework. The agent logic never changes, only where the loop runs.
